💡 Key Takeaways
  • Windows Search gets a makeover, while Hello lights up dim rooms.
  • Microsoft has delivered its final scheduled non-security preview patch of 2026 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2, with an updated Windows Search experience and a brighter Windows Hello for customers who prefer darker rooms.
  • In a recent development, the optional KB5132057 update arrived on November 19, after this month's Patch Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Windows Search gets a makeover, while Hello lights up dim rooms.

Microsoft has delivered its final scheduled non-security preview patch of 2026 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2, with an updated Windows Search experience and a brighter Windows Hello for customers who prefer darker rooms.

In a recent development, the optional KB5132057 update arrived on November 19, after this month's Patch Tuesday. Microsoft is skipping December's non-security preview because of reduced holiday operations, though that doesn't cancel the monthly security release. This last preview is quite a doozy.

Industry observers note that the big-ticket item is the "newly introduced Windows Search Experience." We saw a preview of this last month, and Microsoft has gone well beyond the "just make it work" request of many Windows customers. Results appear faster with less clutter, the tool uses memory better, and files can be previewed directly in Windows Search.

According to recent reports, we're less convinced by inline actions, which let users perform common tasks directly through Windows Search without opening Settings. In our testing, "turn on dark mode" worked, but "switch on dark mode" did not, thus highlighting the limitations of the tool. In addition, we remain unconvinced that Windows Search is the place to run actions.

That mentioned, anything that makes Windows Search less of a punchline for unkind jokes about performance and accuracy is welcome, as are other features, including an optional screen-brightening feature for Windows Hello facial recognition in dim rooms, and the PowerToys-esque Run dialog, which users can enable in Settings.

Industry observers note that while some of the fresh features won't be enabled immediately, Microsoft has included fixes that will be available right away. One addresses an issue where Windows Fax and Scan could fail to connect to a fax server. Handy for those occasions when email falls over into a heap.

There are also fixes for Windows IoT Enterprise LTSC activation failures and the misleading "Something went wrong" message shown on Android devices during cross-device passkey authentication. At the time of writing, Microsoft still lists the problem as something for which "we are working on a resolution to be released in a future Windows revision.".

Sadly, not everything has been pushed off the naughty step. SQL Server queries using OLE DB providers can still leave connections to external databases open after they've finished. Microsoft is working on that one and "will provide an update in an upcoming release." ®.

State of Open Models: Summer 2026 Observations

📅 14 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the AI world, time feels compressed.
  • Industry observers note that models and datasets on HF hub are growing on a daily basis.
  • Recent findings suggest that there used to be a clear progression path: labs would start by releasing smaller models and gradually work their way toward the top end of the scale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the AI world, time feels compressed. A few months after our spring report in our biannual analysis worked through the ecosystem, there are quite a few findings that we have observed until this summer. This report lays out these observations from January to August 2026 and presents the data behind each one.

Industry observers note that models and datasets on HF hub are growing on a daily basis. Public model repositories grew from 2.43 to 2.96 million over the period, datasets from 711,000 to 1 million, Spaces from 1.00 to 1.44 million. The distribution underneath stays extreme, roughly 85.6% of models have fewer than 200 lifetime downloads, and 1.5% of repositories account for 99.2% of all downloads. Everything below happens inside that shape.

Recent findings suggest that there used to be a clear progression path: labs would start by releasing smaller models and gradually work their way toward the top end of the scale. In 2026, several Chinese labs skipped this progression entirely.

Industry observers note that in almost every month of 2026, the largest and most performant open model from a Chinese lab was larger than any model an American lab released. China's monthly ceiling ran between 754B and 2.78 trillion parameters; U.S. models stayed under 130B in five of seven months, the exception being NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Ultra at 561B in May and June, and Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab.

In a recent development, the chart splits the labs into two camps. Moonshot, MiniMax, Xiaomi and Z.ai publish almost nothing below 70B, so a developer's first encounter with them is a model too large to run on anything they own. Tencent and Alibaba Qwen cover the whole range instead, from under 1B upward.

Recent findings suggest that two things made the first camp possible. Building large stopped being a differentiator. Xiaomi, Ant Group and Meituan all cleared a trillion parameters this year, and neither was a household name in open weights twelve months ago. And a lab no longer has to ship a small model to be reachable, because the community's quantization layer will make a large one runnable within days, a dependency we return to below.

In a recent development, that leaves the size profile as a statement of intent rather than of capability. A frontier only portfolio stakes everything on benchmark position and API demand. A full spectrum portfolio is a bid to be the family developers standardise on. Both are rational, they are playing for different prizes.

The United States is not absent from open source.

It has been revealed that the two organizations publishing the most fresh open models this year are also the companies making the hardware: AMD and NVIDIA. Each released more than 200 new model repositories, far ahead of the rest of the field, with LiquidAI ranking third at around 100. Hardware vendors have realized that open models are a way to sell chips: a model optimized for your hardware and freely available is the clearest proof that the hardware works.

Recent findings suggest that when smaller models and embedding models are included, where Google, Microsoft, IBM Granite, and OpenAI’s older vision and speech models generate hundreds of millions of downloads annually, U.S. open source AI is growing.

Industry observers note that more hardware and infrastructure organizations such as NVIDIA are training and open-weighting competitive models. NVIDIA's Nemotron model family boasts high performance. Long-time leaders such as Meta reignite open roots with Meta's Muse Glimmer.

Sources indicate that at the frontier scale, some U.S. model releases above 100B parameters this year are built on top of Chinese models or leverage artifacts from Chinese labs, such as Thinking Machines’ Inkling (952B). Major original American models include NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Ultra (561B), Nemotron 3 Super (124B), and Arcee AI’s Trinity-Large (399B).

It has been revealed that AMD contributed many conversions. This work is crucial: it enables trillion-parameter models to run efficiently on U.S. hardware. This represents a distribution and optimization layer.

Meanwhile, Chinese open models are increasingly optimized for domestic chips in China, the same competition in reverse, where models are designed around specific hardware ecosystems.

We took the top 25 model repositories by downloads accumulated this year and the top 25 by likes. Exactly one repository appears in both lists.

In a recent development, we counted downloads inside the window rather than lifetime, so nothing is credited for merely having existed longer, and controlling for age makes the split sharper. Not one model published in 2026 reaches the download top 25, while thirteen of the twenty-five date from 2022. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 was pulled 1.55 billion times in seven months against 5,156 likes; Kimi-K3 was pulled about 60 times per like it received.

The two numbers record different acts. A like claims a release matters, and goes to frontier models in the weeks after they ship. A download says something is wired into a pipeline that runs on a schedule, and accrues to small, stable models over years. Likes are the right instrument for reading what the field is excited about, downloads for reading what it currently depends on. Treating either as a proxy for the other is the most common mistake we see in coverage of the Hub, including our own earlier work. The same split appears at the level of the publisher.

China's frontier labs are the only accounts on the Hub where the heavy band carries the volume. Effectively all of MiniMax's 2026 downloads are of models above 70B, along with 88% of Moonshot's, 55% of DeepSeek's and 39% of Z.ai's. No large American account looks like this: Google, Microsoft and IBM Granite record essentially none of their 2026 downloads above 70B, and NVIDIA and Meta only 14% and 9%.

Sources indicate that the difference becomes clearer in total downloads. Moonshot’s frontier-only portfolio recorded 37M downloads over the year, while Qwen’s broader release strategy across model sizes reached 2,045M (across repositories with declared parameter counts, 2,061M including all repositories) , about 55 times more. The continued expansion of the family, from the 2.4T-parameter Qwen 3.8 Max to smaller variants such as 27B, reveals the same focus on coverage across different use cases.

Sources indicate that time also plays an crucial role. Most models experience a sharp decline in usage after release, followed by a long tail of steady activity. A model’s adoption is largely determined within its first few months.

This helps explain why today’s download volume is often driven not by the newest releases, but by a smaller group of models that have become established infrastructure over time.

If frontier models were a licensing business, you would expect the biggest releases to carry the tightest terms. However, the data below reveals a different story.

Of 178 Chinese releases above 20B parameters this year, 59% carry Apache 2.0 and 22% carry MIT, and almost none carry non-commercial restrictions. However, in the last few weeks, we started to see a change on this trend for the really large models, with Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 2.4T starting to include some non-commercial restrictions and revenue share requirements to their licenses.

Recent findings suggest that deepSeek and Z.ai ship models between 700 billion and 1.65 trillion parameters under plain MIT. Chinese labs license their largest models about as permissively as their smallest, and more permissively than American labs license theirs: on the American side of the same size band, 29% is Apache or MIT, 41% sits under custom terms and 30% declares nothing at all.

In a recent development, whatever these releases are for, it is not licence revenue. The weights are given away on the most permissive terms available. The return has to come from somewhere else: API and cloud business, hardware and platform positioning, or the ecosystem position itself. For instance, the valuations of Z.ai and Kimi point to an effective open source strategy, getting traction and growth opportunities in the community. Going forward, however, the industry is likely to shift toward clearer monetization paths from open-source adoption.

A model’s ecosystem position is not defined only by its own releases, but by how much the community builds on top of it. As mentioned above, Qwen is one exception which is getting attention and adoption.

By this measure, Qwen has become one of the largest foundations in the open model ecosystem. Qwen-based models now account for 151,448 derivatives on the Hub, 2.6× Meta’s total footprint and 4.7× the Llama repositories specifically. Google follows with 82,506 derivatives. The third-largest source is Unsloth, a community account publishing quantized and fine-tuning-ready builds, many of which further extend the Qwen ecosystem.

According to recent reports, qwen derivatives have increased at roughly 180–210 upcoming repositories per day throughout the first seven months of 2026, showing that adoption is not driven only by individual introduces. Qwen has become part of the default workflow for developers deciding what models to fine-tune and deploy.

Several factors contributed to this position. First, consistency. Qwen has maintained a regular release cadence, continuously updating its model family rather than relying on occasional flagship releases. Second, coverage. It publishes models across a wide range of sizes and use cases, allowing developers to stay within the same ecosystem whether they need a small local model or a larger deployment model. Third, openness. Apache 2.0 licensing reduces friction for modification, redistribution, and commercial use.

It has been revealed that these factors reinforce each other. A broad model family attracts more developers; more developers create more derivatives; and those derivatives make the ecosystem more attractive to future consumers.

This position was built largely by the community. The 151,448 derivatives represent downstream work created by other developers, not releases produced by Qwen itself. Even among the 28,531 GGUF conversions of Qwen models on the Hub, Qwen published only 54.

It has been revealed that among models that declare a parameter count, those under 1B take 83% of all-time downloads and everything above 100B takes 1%. Restricting to downloads accumulated in 2026 changes nothing: 3% of the volume goes to models above 70B. This is the March finding that has held up most cleanly, for the same reason as before, small models are the only ones that run on the hardware most developers actually have.

Industry observers note that so how does a trillion-parameter model reach anyone at all? Through llama.cpp.

According to recent reports, in February the ggml team joined Hugging Face, with the project remaining fully open-source, community-governed and in the same technical direction. What changed is that the most notable project in local inference now has durable resources behind it.

According to recent reports, the ceiling moved with llama.cpp. The July snapshot carries GGUF builds of DeepSeek-V4-Flash at roughly 284B parameters and Kimi-K3 at roughly 2.8 trillion. Local inference used to mean an 8B model on a laptop. It now means a trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts spread across a few consumer machines, which is the alternative route the frontier did not have a year ago, and the reason a frontier-first release strategy is viable at all.

In a recent development, and that route runs on Qwen: 39.6 million GGUF downloads a month, nearly twice Gemma's 20.8 million and more than five times Llama's 7.5 million. The Llama gap is not a supply problem, Llama-derived GGUF repositories slightly outnumber Qwen's. Same shelf space, a fifth of the traffic.

In a recent development, model repositories grew 21.5% over these seven months. Several things around them grew several times faster.

Repositories declaring the gguf library rose 464%, lerobot 194% and Apple's mlx148%, against 16% for transformers and peft and 21% for diffusers. The modelling core is growing at roughly the platform average. The layer that decides where a model can physically run local inference formats, Apple silicon, robot control stacks, is growing three to seven times faster than that.

Across the ten largest model families, the labs behind these models publish very few official GGUF conversions. Yet GGUF versions are often the ones used by developers running models locally. Providing an official conversion at release, documenting quantization choices, and signing the artifacts would require limited additional effort. Rather than maintaining this workflow internally, labs could collaborate with existing ecosystem contributors such as Unsloth. Doing so would narrow the gap between the weights tested by model creators and the versions adopted by the broader community.

We could not have written this section in March, because the instrument did not exist. The agent-usage dataset, published in July, records the agent/ token that coding agents send when they call the Hub through huggingface_hub or the hf CLI — searching for models, pushing datasets, running Jobs, creating Spaces. For the first time we can see how much agent traffic the Hub receives and which harnesses it comes from.

In a recent development, claude Code led July with 44.4%, but a single month conceals the real finding: it held 67.8% in April and 64% in May, while Codex climbed steadily from 10.4% to 20.8%. This is a market with no incumbent, where one release or one changed default can move half the traffic in a month.

Recent findings suggest that the second finding is the unregistered row. Nearly a quarter of agent-tagged traffic in July came from harnesses not yet named in the dataset, and in May that figure was 59.8%. Between April and July more than a dozen fresh client identifiers appeared. New entrants are arriving faster than any registry can name them — which is itself the finding.

Sources indicate that we spent much of the year building for this reader rather than only for human browsers. Papers began serving machine-readable Markdown in March. April brought agent traces as a first-class dataset type and an agents.md endpoint on every Gradio Space, so an agent can read a Space's API and call it directly. July brought the hf_fs tool on our MCP server, exposing repositories, storage, docs and papers through a single interface in just over a thousand tokens, alongside attachable sandboxes for secure execution. The same consolidation happened at the protocol layer, with MCP moving into the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.

Then, in July, an agent stopped being a reader and became an intruder. What appears to be the first documented case of an autonomous agent running a sustained intrusion on its own initiative happened to us. While our team tried to use frontier closed models to analyze the captured attack code, their safety guardrails declined the work. The analysis was completed in the end on a quantized open model GLM-5.2 running on our own infrastructure. We published a disclosure and a full technical timeline.

According to recent reports, compared to the spring report, the geographical rebalancing of power continues to accelerate. While U.S. open source models continue to be competitive, the race between several Chinese frontier model labs draws strong attention. Many likes on these frontier models point to what excites the community the most, and growth opportunity for companies leveraging the attention for valuations.

Sources indicate that however, the AI race is not only sprints, but also a marathon; tools like llama.cpp helps deploying the big models locally, but a broad model family and its adoption is still the key, to build a positive feedback loop between developers, publisher and future users. Models to be embedded in the infrastructure and being part of the ecosystem, may lead to a commercially sound exit at the end of the tunnel.

In the end, with agents being the number 1 user on HF Hub for the first time, the next report may look very different.

In AI, a few months can reshape the ecosystem.

This analysis is based on activity observed on the Hugging Face Hub during the first seven months of 2026.

The metrics used in this report, including downloads, likes, derivatives, and model releases, represent different aspects of ecosystem activity. They should not be interpreted as direct measures of model quality, commercial adoption, or overall market share.

Downloads indicate usage within the Hub ecosystem, but they do not capture API usage, private deployments, or models distributed through other channels.

Likes reflect community attention and interest, while derivative models provide a signal of how much developers build on top of an existing model.

Because open-source AI adoption happens across many channels, Hub activity should be viewed as one perspective on ecosystem development rather than a complete measurement of the AI market.

Tech Report: GitHub availability report: October 2026

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.
  • According to recent reports, the short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate.
  • As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

According to recent reports, the short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

Industry observers note that that capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

In a recent development, we also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in owners. More details on these and other incidents follow.

The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind plan. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Sources indicate that jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

The importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

It has been revealed that duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or issues, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

Web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

It has been revealed that during regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One new machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

Industry observers note that customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

In a recent development, customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, fresh commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

Industry observers note that audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

Some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, newly introduced connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

Sources indicate that we took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the matter.

Audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

Sources indicate that customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

Copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 9 minutes.

It has been revealed that customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Issues, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. Fresh requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

Industry observers note that the pool was already running near capacity when some upgrade requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Sources indicate that follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

Today, we laid out our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive, end-to-end software delivery system in the world.

#23730. Same Cluster, 33 Points More Utilization: What Changed Was the Order

📅 17 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2650 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Same Cluster, 33 Points More Utilization: What Changed Was the Order

📅 17 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The previous post argued that utilization, not intelligence, is where the next real constraint in enterprise AI is forming, and it closed by noting that no playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like.
  • We built a constraint-aware GPU allocator and benchmarked it against a FIFO scheduler across seven benchmark scenarios.
  • One note on measurement before the numbers start.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The previous post argued that utilization, not intelligence, is where the next real constraint in enterprise AI is forming, and it closed by noting that no playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. This is ours.

We built a constraint-aware GPU allocator and benchmarked it against a FIFO scheduler across seven benchmark scenarios. On identical hardware, running identical workloads, GPU utilization rose by as much as 33 percentage points, and priority-weighted output rose in every one of them, by as much as 105%. Nothing about the hardware changed. What changed was the order in which allocation decisions get made.

One note on measurement before the numbers start. Every gain below is expressed as improvement over the FIFO result on the same scenario. Utilization is reported in percentage points; value is reported as a percentage increase in priority-weighted output.

"Keep the GPUs busy" is not a decision a system can execute. The decision is narrower and much harder: which GPU runs which job, in which timestep, at what priority. Formally it is one binary choice per combination of GPU, job and timestep, and the output is a grid — every GPU, across the whole scheduling horizon, with a job name in each cell or nothing at all.

Recent findings suggest that four workload types compete for that grid: training, real-time inference, batch inference, and quantization. They split into two allocation shapes, and the split is where the difficulty lives. Training, batch inference and quantization are batch-like: once started, each needs a contiguous block of GPUs held without interruption until the job finishes. Real-time inference is the opposite: elastic, driven by a demand curve that changes every timestep, growing and shrinking as traffic does.

Two incompatible shapes competing for the same hardware in the same timestep is the core problem. A second heterogeneity sits inside a single type: for the same base model, training jobs range from a few hours to several days, and from one GPU to dozens.

The comparison point throughout is a FIFO-based scheduler: real-time inference served from a fixed reservation, and every other job placed in arrival order, without regard for priority.

Under the right conditions, that is a reasonable policy. When the cluster has slack, allocation order costs nothing in utilization, everything fits regardless of sequence, so FIFO and anything more sophisticated fill the same fraction of the pool. Contention is where that ordering cost stops being invisible and starts costing capacity too. It then becomes expensive in two separate ways, and they are worth taking one at a time.

Industry observers note that the reservation. Real-time inference cannot wait for capacity; the GPUs have to be there the moment traffic needs them. A scheduler that places jobs in arrival order has no mechanism for releasing GPUs during a trough and reclaiming them before the next peak, so the only way to guarantee availability is to take each real-time application's maximum demand for the day and reserve that many GPUs for the whole day. The cost lands in every hour that is not the peak. An application needing six GPUs at midday and two at 4am holds all six for twenty-four hours, and the four idle GPUs are unavailable to any batch job for the entire day. They are not being used, and they are not free either. It is why the baseline sits near half the cluster in the two scenarios where reservation dominates: 51.6% in the mixed control and 53.6% in the training-heavy case. Roughly half a pool, with much of the idle half reserved rather than free. This cost is paid whether the cluster is contended or not — contention only makes it visible.

The ordering. Under real contention, which jobs fit at all depends on the order you place them, not just on how much capacity exists. Order is not a tiebreaker applied after the capacity question is settled. Order is a capacity decision. FIFO places each job as it arrives, without weighing what that job is worth and without checking what else still has to fit inside the horizon, so high-priority work waits behind whatever asked first and capacity gets committed in placements that later jobs cannot use.

Industry observers note that the two compound. The block held for the day's maximum real-time demand is off the table for every batch job in the queue, in every hour, and whatever remains is handed out in the order the requests happened to arrive.

It is the GPU equivalent of an airline assigning aircraft to whichever charter called first, then finding nothing left to fly the route that actually pays. And GPUs reserved all day for a peak lasting a couple of hours are the grounded aircraft from the previous piece in the most literal sense: on standby, earning nothing, unavailable to anyone else.

[Figure: side-by-side allocation grids — allocator above, FIFO below, same scenario].

Across five benchmark scenarios built for genuine contention, the allocator improved both axes at once. Utilization moved from a 52–85% band to a 72–88% band. Priority-weighted value rose between 24.6% and 105.1%, averaging 52%. Every scenario, both metrics, no tradeoff to explain away.

The strongest single case was a training-heavy workload on 8 GPUs: utilization went from 53.6% to 87.0%, and value more than doubled, up 105%. Thirty-three points of a fixed, already-depreciating asset, recovered by reclaiming reserved standby capacity and placing the rest in priority order. (This figure reflect a single baseline ordering.).

The allocator removes both behaviors. Real-time demand is treated as a curve rather than a ceiling, allocated against demand at each timestep, with batch-like work occupying the troughs, bounded by the cap on how many GPUs a real-time job may swap between consecutive timesteps. And batch-like jobs are placed by priority across the whole horizon instead of in the order they arrived. The rest of this piece is how.

Utilization measures occupancy: what fraction of available GPU-time is allocated to something. It carries no information about what that something is worth. One scenario pulls the two apart completely, and the gap runs in a direction that is easy to miss.

In the scale test, 30 jobs across 64 GPUs, FIFO and the allocator produced identical utilization, 44.9% each, and identical throughput, 27 of 30 jobs completed. The allocator delivered 15.9% more priority-weighted value. Every dashboard reads the same. The cluster produced materially different output.

An objective that does not price priority can fill the cluster to exactly the same level, finish exactly as many jobs, and still deliver less. The previous piece argued that occupancy is a poor read on whether a cluster is earning; this is the measured version of that claim.

The alternative is not a longer list of heuristic rules. Some constraints only mean anything globally, and no local rule can express them: contiguous blocks, a budget for how much GPU churn is acceptable across the entire horizon, a guarantee that running work is never preempted. To honor those, the problem has to be written down as one thing.

Five constraints define a legal allocation:.

In a recent development, the objective function has two terms. Allocating a GPU to a batch-like job earns a reward equal to its priority multiplied by a time-decay weight. Failing to meet real-time demand incurs a penalty proportional to the size of the shortfall.

The relative size of those weights is the entire service-level policy, expressed as one number. The real-time penalty weight is 5 to 10 times greater than the allocation weight. One unit of unmet real-time demand therefore costs what 5 to 10 GPU-timesteps of equal-priority batch work costs. The asymmetry is deliberate, and it means latency obligations are enforced inside the same optimization that places batch work, rather than by a separate autoscaler competing with the scheduler for the same GPUs.

Recent findings suggest that it is also what makes the elastic treatment of real-time demand safe. The allocator can hand a GPU to batch work during a trough because underserving real-time demand later is priced so far above whatever that batch work earns — the penalty, not a static reservation, is what protects availability.

The time weight decays across the horizon for a reason that only makes sense in an online system: by the next scheduling run, latest jobs will have arrived. Capacity used now is worth more than capacity promised later.

The formal model defines what a legal, well-scored allocation looks like. Answering an incoming request is a separate job, and it belongs to a separate component. This is NP-hard combinatorial allocation, and the scheduler is re-invoked every time a job arrives, so the decision has to come back in the gap between two API requests. That latency budget is the fixed constraint the architecture is designed around, which is why a heuristic sits on the hot path and the formal model sits behind it as the specification the heuristic is built to satisfy.

Sources indicate that that heuristic is not a generic greedy allocator. Its rules are the formal model's structural constraints, which means every grid it produces is a legal allocation by construction. Not usually valid. Valid by design.

Sources indicate that that design, applied across the whole horizon rather than one arrival at a time, is what produces the utilization gain. The allocator sees every queued job before it places any of them, it can hold the free pool in shapes the remaining work can actually occupy, a batch job needing a contiguous block of a given size still has room when its turn comes. Priority decides who gets first claim on that room. FIFO has neither view: it commits capacity to whichever job asked first, and a job that arrives later and needs a specific shape may find nothing left that fits, so it goes unscheduled and the GPU-hours it would have consumed go unclaimed.

It runs in 1 to 2 milliseconds on the five contended scenarios, and 15 milliseconds at 64 GPUs and 30 jobs — fast enough to run on every incoming request.

Sources indicate that the system exposes two modes. Fast mode runs the allocator alone and returns its grid; this is the hot path. Full mode uses that grid as a starting point for the formal model, which attempts to improve on it — suited to periodic review rather than per-request decisions.

Utilization improved in every scenario but one, where it tied exactly. Value improved in all seven.

The scale test matters because it holds at size: 64 GPUs, 30 jobs, 15 milliseconds, 15.9% more value.

Industry observers note that the uniform-priority test matters because it addresses the obvious skeptical reading. Override every job to identical priority, so that no priority signal distinguishes any of them, and the allocator still moves utilization from 76.8% to 87.5% and value up 23.1%. The gain is not purely an artifact of ordering by priority. Planning placements across the horizon contributes on its own.

According to recent reports, everything above assumes the scheduler knows how many GPU-hours each job needs and how much real-time traffic is coming. Both are predictions, not inputs, and a scheduler is only as good as they are.

A single generic estimator does not work, because the four workload types have qualitatively different cost drivers. This is where the specialization argument from the previous piece reconnects: the same logic that makes a task-specific model outperform a generalist applies to the estimators feeding the scheduler.

Training is not one workload. It varies along two independent, freely combinable axes. Strategy determines how much of the model is updated (full fine-tuning against parameter-efficient methods like LoRA). Technique determines the optimization objective and the training loop (SFT, DPO, RLHF, RLVR, CPT). The differences are not marginal: LoRA cuts trainable parameters by up to 10,000× and GPU memory roughly 3× against full fine-tuning, on the same base model. DPO removes both the reward model and the sampling loop of RLHF. Estimating from model size alone averages across runs that differ by orders of magnitude, in exactly the two quantities the scheduler decides on, duration and GPU count. Our training forecaster conditions on 22 features, including a categorical variable distinguishing 10 concrete training variants.

According to recent reports, quantization is a schedulable job, not a background chore. Quantizing a single large model can consume hours of GPU time on hardware that other work is waiting for. It gets its own forecast, built from calibration tiers by parameter count, with distinct handling per algorithm (bitsandbytes, AWQ, GPTQ) and a safety margin before rounding up to whole GPU-hours. Prior work in this area places quantization outside scheduling scope entirely.

Real-time inference is not estimated per job at all. It is forecast as a continuously recalibrated weekly demand profile, rebuilt from hourly traffic history and mapped to GPU counts under the same swap cost the formal model enforces. Forecast and optimizer therefore agree on what churn costs, rather than disagreeing and fighting each other. This forecast is what replaces peak reservation. A per-timestep demand curve is the only thing that lets the scheduler release GPUs during a trough with any confidence that they can be reclaimed before the next peak.

Recent findings suggest that this closes back to the ordering argument. Better demand estimates are what make priority-aware placement possible in the first place, you cannot sequence jobs well without knowing what they will consume.

According to recent reports, the obvious objection to all of this is that forecasts are wrong. What happens then?

The failure mode to avoid has a name worth borrowing: the end-of-world effect. An optimizer that cannot see past the end of its horizon makes present decisions that wreck the timesteps immediately outside it, because as far as the model is concerned, nothing exists after the horizon ends.

Industry observers note that the architecture answers both problems at once. The scheduler optimizes a 24-hour horizon, but commits only the current timestep, and re-runs every 30 to 60 minutes. Run at 9am, and the 9am allocation is real; the strategy for 10am through 5pm exists only so that the 9am decision is made by a model that knows a future exists. The real 10am allocation comes from the 10am run, against fresh data.

Sources indicate that the consequence is that forecast error is absorbed by re-optimization instead of compounding. Each run inherits what is actually running and pins it in place, so successive prepares upgrade rather than thrash.

There is a secondary payoff. The horizon proposal is itself a forecasting product: it surfaces real-time coverage risk and predictable idle windows before they arrive, which is useful whether or not those specific allocations are ever committed.

It has been revealed that this is also why the time-decay weight exists. By the next run, the workload mix will have changed.

Sources indicate that airlines did not solve utilization by computing an optimal schedule. They solved it by encoding operational discipline into the order things happen (turnaround sequence, maintenance windows, crew rostering) and letting that discipline compound.

The same thing happened here. Thirty-three points of utilization in the hardest-packed scenario, and 52% more priority-weighted output on average, on the same hardware, with the same workloads, in a couple of milliseconds, came from encoding what the cluster physically permits into the order decisions get made. Structure beat sophistication.

The previous piece argued that specialization and orchestration are two halves of one problem: specialization shrinks what each workload needs, and orchestration decides where the difference goes. Neither lever pays off alone. This is what the second half looks like when it is built.

It has been revealed that the GPUs were already installed, already committed, already depreciating. The gain was in how we chose to spend them.

AI boom threatens circuit board crunch to rival pandemic-era chip shortage

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Trade body warns automotive, medical, and defense orders are being crowded out, with relief unlikely before mid-2028.
  • The electronics industry faces a printed circuit board (PCB) shortage that could rival the pandemic-era chip crunch – with AI once again accused of hogging supplies.
  • The Global Electronics Association claims demand is arriving "at a scale the supply chain was not built for," straining everything from glass fabric and resin to finished boards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Trade body warns automotive, medical, and defense orders are being crowded out, with relief unlikely before mid-2028.

The electronics industry faces a printed circuit board (PCB) shortage that could rival the pandemic-era chip crunch – with AI once again accused of hogging supplies.

The Global Electronics Association claims demand is arriving "at a scale the supply chain was not built for," straining everything from glass fabric and resin to finished boards.

Industry observers note that its report, "The PCB Squeeze: A Wake-Up Call for Global Electronics," notes AI servers need increasingly complex boards. While a typical PC board has about 12 layers of tracks, AI server boards can have 40 to 60 layers or more, and each additional layer requires more resin, copper foil, and laminate.

The supply of materials is set to be constrained through at least the first half of 2027, the report notes, with meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028.

Programs to deliver PCBs for automotive, industrial, medical and even the defense industries are being crowded out as AI soaks up scarce capacity, it claims.

The association's North American figures show orders growing much faster than deliveries. PCB bookings rose 56.1 percent in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, while PCB shipments increased 13.3 percent.

Recent findings suggest that fabrication capacity is expanding, aimed at meeting the increased demand from the AI infrastructure sector, especially in Asia, where more than 90 percent of the world's boards are made. The report says that $10 billion has gone toward fresh PCB plants in Southeast Asia, and at least as much has been invested in China over the past three years, but the raw materials are themselves constrained.

Industry observers note that it warns of lengthening lead times for those raw materials. Standard FR-4 laminate now takes six to eight weeks to ship, up from two to three weeks a year ago, while advanced low-loss laminates now take 14 to 18 weeks for delivery, for example.

Tightening supplies usually lead to price increases, and the report states that suppliers raised laminate costs by 30 percent in September, and that the price tag of some types of E-glass cloth for circuit boards has risen by 300 percent.

In a recent development, the report also puts copper prices up 37 percent over the past year. Concerns have been raised about copper supplies before, as The Register has reported multiple times.

The association compares the risk with the 2021 chip shortage, when disrupted supplies left manufacturers unable to secure even relatively mundane components.

New capacity is coming, but it is late and comes in dribs and drabs, according to the report, while AI demand just keeps on absorbing it as soon as it arrives.

Recent findings suggest that the association's advice is for buyers to plan early, and to share realistic forecasts with suppliers rather than double-booking. Board makers should qualify alternative suppliers of materials such as laminate and copper foil before shortages bite, but it warns against stockpiling beyond real need, which adds to forward-buying pressure.

But it would like governments to step in, of course, by tracking board and material lead times with industry and offering tax incentives for investment in advanced PCB and substrate manufacturing equipment.

Sources indicate that the wish list also includes state investment in research and development plus qualification of latest alternative materials. It would like to see loan guarantees and grants to protect critical programs and small fabricators, structured so as to sustain new capacity if forward buying unravels and demand corrects in 2027.

"Yes, we are seeing constraint in upstream materials and have been reporting it for the past couple of quarters," remarked Cori Masters, senior research analyst director for Supply Chain Operations at Gartner.

In a recent development, "In addition, AI datacenter infrastructure build out is moving capacity support to high-layer count PCBs which increase throughput time and decreases availability of line utilization for more traditional PCB products," she told The Register. ®.
