📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

Industry observers note that AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly vital sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

According to recent reports, this builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

It has been revealed that transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve reveals the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

Industry observers note that the coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

It has been revealed that once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

Sources indicate that the BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.
  • Last week, Microsoft shipped ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 as part of the wider .NET 11 release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News .NET 11 : ASP.NET Core: Union Type Support, OpenAPI 3.2 by Default and Blazor AI Components.

Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.

Last week, Microsoft shipped ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 as part of the wider .NET 11 release. The update spans Minimal APIs, OpenAPI, SignalR, Blazor, authentication, and the Kestrel server. As stated in the announcement, .NET 11 is a Standard Term Support release with two years of support.

It has been revealed that on the API side, developers can now use C# 15 union types in JSON request and response bodies across Minimal APIs and MVC. The release notes limit the feature to JSON bodies, so route, query, header, and form values cannot bind to a union.

Recent findings suggest that minimal API validation also runs asynchronous validators, which keeps threads free while a rule waits on a database lookup or a remote call. The framework can now localize validation messages and display names itself, and endpoints can skip the remaining middleware pipeline through a new [ShortCircuit] attribute.

In a recent development, developers who generate OpenAPI documents now get version 3.2 unless they select an earlier one for tooling that has not caught up. As described in the release notes, the framework depends on Microsoft.OpenApi 3.3.1 for this, and the notes label that upgrade a breaking change.

Recent findings suggest that with 3.2, endpoints that stream server-sent events are documented with a schema for each event's payload, and the generator emits an anyOf schema for unions. Generated documents can also describe endpoints that use the HTTP QUERY method, and APIs that carry the [Obsolete] attribute show up as deprecated.

Recent findings suggest that signalR adds authentication refresh, so a long-lived connection no longer has to close when its access token expires. As reported, server developers enable it per hub, while the .NET client refreshes automatically by default and the TypeScript client can do the same. Blazor passes the refreshed identity on to Interactive Server components while the circuit stays connected.

Blazor receives the longest list of changes, and many of them target static server-side rendering. With the latest CacheView component, developers can cache the rendered markup of a component subtree, and the child components do not run when a cached copy is served. Blazor now ships client-side validation for static SSR forms, enabled by default.

Sources indicate that developers can also carry data between requests with TempData or session values. According to the release notes, the Blazor Web App template drops its app.UseAntiforgery() call, because a middleware for CSRF protection is now added by default.

Industry observers note that for Interactive Server apps, an opt-in package pauses the circuit of a hidden browser tab after a delay, two minutes by default, to free server memory. Lists built with Virtualize may now mix items of different heights, and Microsoft raised the default OverscanCount from 3 to 15. Page and sort state in QuickGrid now lives in the URL query string, with sortable headers and pager controls rendered as links instead of buttons.

According to recent reports, the release notes flag this as a CSS breaking change, because custom styles written for the buttons also have to target the links. The release also includes Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.AI, a set of components for chat and agent interfaces. According to the announcement, Microsoft treats that package as experimental and will keep it in prerelease throughout .NET 11.

On the security and server side, an experimental package adds Device Bound Session Credentials, a protocol that ties session refresh to a private key held by the browser. Response compression and request decompression gain Zstandard support, which is on by default.

Kestrel's HTTP/1.1 parser no longer throws exceptions on malformed requests, a change that is reported to raise throughput by up to 20 to 40 percent under heavy invalid traffic. The shared framework libraries of ASP.NET Core are now compiled with runtime-async, described in the release notes as an internal change with no public API impact.

Two older APIs are on the way out. The Microsoft.AspNetCore.Grpc.Swagger package is now deprecated, and Kestrel's TlsClientHelloBytesCallback option is obsolete in favor of the fresh UseTlsClientHelloListener extension.

Other changes in this release are native OpenTelemetry tracing attributes, client-side cancellation of SignalR hub invocations, scrolling to a specific item in Virtualize and QuickGrid, passkey display names inferred from the authenticator, and TimeProvider support in ASP.NET Core Identity.

For interested readers and developers, the full release notes are available in the What's new in ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 article on Microsoft Learn.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, reinforcement Learning environments give latest capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents.
  • Sources indicate that an environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome.
  • Industry observers note that an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the upcoming RL Environments filter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, reinforcement Learning environments give latest capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

Sources indicate that an environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

Industry observers note that an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the upcoming RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Recent findings suggest that every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a newly introduced paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

According to recent reports, we think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it.".

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:.

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

According to recent reports, the command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:.

It has been revealed that A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

It has been revealed that neMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:.

It has been revealed that that is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

The docs have the full reference.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

It has been revealed that the first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:.

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

In a recent development, if you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.
  • We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018.
  • In a recent development, rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort.

Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. New contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...].

In a recent development, rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that holo4 is our new series of agentic models.
  • According to recent reports, holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs.
  • Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

According to recent reports, holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Industry observers note that holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

It has been revealed that holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

📅 29 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1827 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage.
  • Sources indicate that our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap.
  • Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Sources indicate that our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern shows up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

According to recent reports, this is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

ProvenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

The verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

In a recent development, A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a new setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

We tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts said 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

According to recent reports, binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an notable area for improvement.

It has been revealed that we also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This demonstrates it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

In a recent development, that adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

It has been revealed that want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Industry observers note that source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Sources indicate that practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval claims "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the glitch well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;.

Industry observers note that like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

According to recent reports, hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

Recent findings suggest that however, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Use AI to Multiply Your Team as a Staff Engineer.

Nov 19, 2026 4 min read.

It has been revealed that at QCon San Francisco 2026, Jordan Cutler, Senior Staff Engineer and Web Platform Tech Lead at Pinterest, presented how the role of a staff engineer changes when every engineer has access to the same AI tools. The session argued that most "AI for engineers" content focuses on individual productivity, while the real question for staff engineers is where their leverage comes from now. According to Cutler, AI did not change what a staff engineer is for, but it changed where the leverage is.

According to recent reports, the talk opened with a reflection on Cutler's previous conference talk, where he showed how AI could turn a four-hour task into four minutes. At that point he was shipping roughly as much as his whole team, which he described as multiplying himself rather than his team. That framed the central question of the session: what does a 10x engineer look like when everyone has AI?

In a recent development, to illustrate why this matters, Cutler shared internal Pinterest data on merged pull requests per engineer per week between Q1 2025 and Q3 2026. The top 10% of engineers went from 6.7 to 11.3 merged PRs per week, a 68% increase, while the bottom half went from 1.0 to 1.15, an increase of 14%. Everyone has AI, but not everyone uses it the same way, and the gap keeps growing. The presentation organized the response to that gap into three moves: multiply yourself, multiply your team, and multiply the system.

The first move, multiply yourself, is about going first. Cutler explained that he tries new tools before his team does, and that part of that work is hitting dead ends so others don't have to. He mentioned examples such as an agent harness that could not be steered mid-task and a remote agent runner that required too many follow-ups. Sharing those findings early means the team does not lose a week on the same experiments. Running many agents also revealed a new problem: he kept giving the same corrections in every session, such as avoiding em-dashes, adding a diagram to the PR description, and keeping pull requests small.

The second move, multiply your team, started from a limitation: the folder made him faster, but only he had it. With upcoming people joining the team and a new area to ramp up on, Cutler found himself repeating the same comments in code review, such as asking why a value is null instead of fixing the cause, testing like a user would, and keeping PRs small. The talk emphasized that the value of encoding that judgment grows with every teammate who adopts it, compared to the flat curve of a single engineer working alone.

The third move, multiply the system, is about moving up a level. Cutler used the history of container shipping as an analogy: ports got better at loading cargo by hand, but the standard box changed the economics entirely, from $5.86 a ton to 16 cents a ton. At Pinterest, migrations were the cargo, one kind of change spread across hundreds of files and dozens of teams. Instead of running each migration by hand, the team built a system where a staff engineer points to a initiative and an example, an engineer puts it on a schedule, and an agent running in a sandbox splits the work into PRs team by team. A class component migration ran three to five times faster than by hand, in the background while teams worked on other things.

Sources indicate that the talk also covered what went wrong. One scheduled job looped and opened 16 PRs in two minutes, increasing CI wait times from under 30 seconds to 14 minutes. The lesson was not to wait for the perfect guardrail, but to ship a small one. Cutler encouraged attendees to find their own "any" problem: a first responder for any incident, a draft fix for any bug ticket, or an agent that triages any flaky test. Today, 40 engineers have scheduler jobs of their own.

Sources indicate that the results were significant. Using the same AI tools as other web teams, Cutler's team now ships about four times as much per engineer, without counting his own PRs.

Recent findings suggest that the presentation concluded with practical steps: write down what you repeat, put it where people already work, and build for every case instead of one. Some parts of the job cannot be written down, like an honest conversation with a teammate who is struggling, and those remain the staff engineer's responsibility. As Cutler put it, a 10x engineer isn't ten times faster, they are the reason ten other people are. As AI agents become part of everyday development workflows, the role of senior engineers may increasingly shift from personal output toward encoding judgment into the tools, defaults, and systems that entire organizations use.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Compound interest is often called the eighth wonder of the world, and for good reason.
  • According to recent reports, here is the core concept.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Compound interest is often called the eighth wonder of the world, and for good reason. It is the mathematical force that turns consistent, modest investing into life-changing wealth — and it is the foundation of every financial independence plan.

According to recent reports, here is the core concept. Simple interest earns a return only on your original deposit. If you invest $10,000 at 7% simple interest, you earn $700 per year — every year, forever, on the same $10,000 base. After 30 years, you would have $31,000.

Industry observers note that compound interest earns a return on your original deposit plus all the interest previously earned. In Year 1, you earn $700 on your $10,000. In Year 2, you earn 7% on $10,700 — that is $749. In Year 3, you earn 7% on $11,449 — that is $801. Each year, your interest earns its own interest, and the growth accelerates.

In a recent development, after 30 years of compound interest at 7%, your $10,000 grows to approximately $76,123 — more than double the $31,000 from simple interest. And that is with a single $10,000 deposit and no additional contributions.

It has been revealed that the difference starts small and then explodes. In the first 10 years, compound interest adds only $2,672 more than simple interest. In the last 10 years (year 20 to 30), it adds over $30,000 more. This accelerating curve is why time in the market matters more than almost any other factor in building wealth.

Investing $500 per month at a 7% average annual return — roughly the inflation-adjusted historical return of the S&P 500 — produces dramatically different results depending on how long you invest. After 10 years: $86,500. After 20 years: $260,500. After 30 years: $567,000. You contribute $180,000 of your own money over 30 years. Compound interest adds $387,000 — more than double your contributions. Time is the multiplier that no amount of additional savings can replace.

The compound interest formula is straightforward once you understand the components:.

For a $10,000 investment at 7% compounded monthly for 30 years:.

A = 10,000 x (1 + 0.07/12)^(12 x 30) = 10,000 x (1.00583)^360 = $81,165.

Notice this is higher than the $76,123 from annual compounding — more frequent compounding produces slightly more growth, though the difference is modest.

The jump from annual to monthly compounding is meaningful. The jump from monthly to daily is negligible. Most bank accounts and investment returns compound daily or monthly, so you are already getting nearly the maximum benefit.

It has been revealed that the Rule of 72 is the single most useful mental math shortcut in personal finance. Divide 72 by your expected annual return to estimate how many years it takes to double your money.

According to recent reports, at a 7% real return, your money doubles every 10 years. A $100,000 portfolio at age 25 becomes $200,000 at 35, $400,000 at 45, and $800,000 at 55 — even with zero additional contributions. This is why starting early is the single most powerful financial decision you can make.

It has been revealed that if you use a nominal return of 10% instead, the numbers look even more dramatic, but they overstate your future purchasing power. Always use inflation-adjusted returns (6-7%) for retirement planning and real purchasing power comparisons.

Consider two investors. Investor A starts investing $500 per month at age 25 and stops at age 35 — investing for only 10 years, then letting it grow untouched until age 65. Investor B waits until age 35 and invests $500 per month every month from 35 to 65 — investing for 30 years.

Recent findings suggest that investor A contributes one-third the money and ends up with more at 65. The 10-year head start gave compound interest enough time to overcome the difference. This is not a trick — it is the fundamental math of compounding. Every year you delay costs you more than the money you eventually invest.

Put the math to work starting today.

According to recent reports, the single most important factor in compound interest is time, not amount. Even $100 per month started today beats $500 per month started five years from now over a long enough timeline. Open a brokerage account or increase your 401(k) contribution today.

Pro tip: Automate your contributions so they happen before you see the money in your checking account.

According to recent reports, the historical 7-10% average return comes from broad stock market index funds. A total US stock market fund or S&P 500 fund with an expense ratio below 0.10% gives you the full benefit of compound growth without high fees eroding your returns.

When you get a raise, increase your monthly investment by at least half the raise amount. This prevents lifestyle inflation from consuming your additional income and accelerates compound growth.

Pro tip: A 3% annual raise invested means your contributions grow exponentially alongside your investment returns.

Industry observers note that set all your accounts to automatically reinvest dividends. Dividend reinvestment is compound interest within compound interest — your dividends buy more shares, which generate more dividends, which buy more shares.

Market downturns are not a reason to sell — they are the cost of admission for long-term compound growth. Every major market crash in history has been followed by recovery and latest highs. Pulling money out during a downturn and reinvesting later is the most reliable way to destroy compound interest.

Pro tip: If seeing your balance drop causes panic, check your portfolio less frequently. Quarterly or annually is enough.

Recent findings suggest that simple interest is calculated only on your original principal. Compound interest is calculated on your principal plus all previously earned interest. Over long periods, the difference is enormous — $10,000 at 7% for 30 years grows to $31,000 with simple interest but $76,123 with compound interest.

More frequent compounding produces slightly higher returns, but the difference is small. Monthly compounding at 7% on $10,000 for 30 years yields $81,165 versus $76,123 for annual compounding — a difference of about 6.6%. Most investment accounts compound daily or when dividends are reinvested, so you are already receiving near-optimal compounding.

Yes. Compound interest (more accurately, compound growth) applies to any investment account where your returns are reinvested. In a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account invested in index funds, your gains generate additional gains. Tax-advantaged accounts like Roth IRAs are especially powerful because the compounding occurs entirely tax-free.

It has been revealed that the S&P 500 has returned approximately 10% annually in nominal terms over the past century. Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7%. For conservative planning, use 6-7% to account for inflation. For nominal calculations (not inflation-adjusted), use 9-10%. Using rates above 10% for long-term projections is overly optimistic for a diversified portfolio.

Industry observers note that yes — and the math is surprisingly accessible. Investing $1,000 per month at a 7% real return reaches $1,134,000 in 30 years (you contribute $360,000, compound interest adds $774,000). At $500 per month, you reach $567,000 in 30 years. The key variables are consistent contribution, a reasonable return, and patience.

Recent findings suggest that compound interest is the mathematical engine behind financial independence. The FI community uses compound growth to accumulate 25x their annual expenses in invested assets (the 4% rule). By saving 50%+ of income and investing in index funds that compound at 7-10% annually, FIRE practitioners can reach financial independence in 10-17 years rather than the traditional 40-year career.

Recent findings suggest that compound interest is the most powerful wealth-building force available to ordinary investors. The math is unambiguous: $500 per month at 7% becomes $567,000 in 30 years, with compound interest contributing more than twice what you personally invest. The two factors you control — how much you invest and how long you stay invested — matter far more than picking the "right" stocks or timing the market. Start today, invest in low-cost index funds, reinvest all dividends, and do not interrupt the compounding. Time is your greatest asset, and every year you wait costs more than you think.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Serpentine ↗ Open Full Page

Announcing jj-musubi: live sync for Jujutsu

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Serpentine

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m pleased to announce a latest source control tool, jj-musubi, that live-syncs copies of a Jujutsu (jj) repository across multiple machines.
  • jj-musubi makes repos on multiple machines feel like jj workspaces (worktrees if you speak git).
  • It’s intended for use by one person who works across several machines, so it has no security model (or rather, that is the extent of its security model).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m pleased to announce a latest source control tool, jj-musubi, that live-syncs copies of a Jujutsu (jj) repository across multiple machines. Every time jj snapshots my work, jj-musubi syncs it to every machine in moments, and also commits, rebases, fetches, and so on.

This simple capability is surprisingly powerful.

jj-musubi makes repos on multiple machines feel like jj workspaces (worktrees if you speak git).

It’s intended for use by one person who works across several machines, so it has no security model (or rather, that is the extent of its security model).

Jujutsu already treats the working copy as a commit. Running jj status records a snapshot of my edits in that commit, which jj-musubi then syncs to my other machines. I like to have my shell prompt run jj status, so in practice I rarely have to think about snapshots.

Sources indicate that jj-musubi does not write to the working copy. Each machine has its own working copy and workspaces as usual, so syncs of commits, snapshots, and rewrites can bring in fresh history while a build is running, without changing the files under it. On a laptop, I can work offline, and my machine will sync when I’m back on the network.

Industry observers note that this has also proven handy when I have agents working on several machines. I can give each agent its own jj workspace on different systems, then run jj diff -r devbox/agent-1@ on the laptop to see what one of them has done so far. If one finds a bug that another needs to fix, they can coordinate and see each other’s work without overhead.

jj-musubi refers to a collection of copies of a repo as a hive.

Industry observers note that I often run agents in temporary disposable VMs. jj-musubi supports this by allowing an agent to lease its repo’s membership in the hive: if it doesn’t renew that lease in time, its repo gets forgotten about, so temporary repos or vanished containers can’t just stack up and clutter things.

According to recent reports, back when I was at Meta, I kicked off the project that became Sapling and Mononoke. Sapling’s Commit Cloud gives engineers there a similar way to move work between machines, and Google engineers have something similar with an internal jj server.

In a recent development, since then, I’d missed that everyday convenience for the machines I already use, and felt like I could get it without massive infrastructure or hosting. With jj-musubi, one machine runs a hub, and daemons exchange jj history with it over SSH. That’s almost as lightweight as you can get.

It has been revealed that what’s tricky is getting concurrent work right. That’s already hard in any distributed source control system, and when syncs are live and we plan for disconnected work in an unreliable network, the difficulty goes way up.

As a user, I shouldn’t have to care about when exactly I can safely close my laptop after finishing an edit; all of my changes should make it through either just before I close it, or right after I reopen. No work should get lost or corrupted in the presence of interrupts, resends, delays, or machines sleeping, and the system should stay reliable even when machines go offline forever.

I used Lean to prove key properties of jj-musubi’s network protocol, and tests compare the Rust code against that model. An extensive body of other tests run real jj repositories through concurrent edits, interrupted syncs, hub restarts, and a myriad of other nasty situations. Mutation and adversarial testing ensure that when bugs are injected, sensible things happen. The safety guide details all the checks (and the parts I don’t yet cover).

It might sound spooky or dangerous to be able to see in-progress work on one machine from another. How can that be safe?

If you use jj in multiple workspaces, you’re already used to the novelty of being able to check out the same change in two workspaces and modify it. jj simply marks the change as divergent, but it won’t update either working copy with changes from the other until you decide to, e.g. by calling jj workspace update-stale. In jj, dealing with divergent versions of a change is similar to any other kind of conflicted merge.

It has been revealed that jj-musubi uses jj’s existing workspace machinery, so everything will feel familiar. The only difference is that when you run jj-musubi, a workspace’s name is prefixed with the name of the machine it lives on.

Sources indicate that start with e.g. a laptop and another machine that’s always on (let’s call it devbox), with a copy of a jj repo on each. On each machine, download the binary or build it yourself:.

In a recent development, run musubi hub on devbox; it will keep your sync data in ~/musubi-hub. In the laptop’s repo, run musubi create --hub devbox. In devbox’s repo, run musubi join.

Sources indicate that I provide builds for Linux, macOS and Windows, and the quick start walks through setup and the first sync. If you try it and something surprises you, I’d like to hear about it.

It has been revealed that my name is Renato Losio. I'm an editor at InfoQ. I'm joined today by four experts coming from different companies, different sectors, different countries. Recent findings suggest that gunnar Grosch: I'm Gunnar. I'm a developer advocate at Sinch. These days, I build and talk a lot about AI agents in production, and working with Sinch, obviously that means a lot of conversational AI in different ways. I also have a podcast with some friends, called, Yells at Cloud.

Industry observers note that renato Losio: How is AI already changing software delivery in your organization? We are all familiar with developers using coding assistants. We're putting knowledge back somewhere in skills and more information, so the agents become better. We improve the harness. That's all good. I would call that our solo level, team shared level working together. About six or seven months ago, we switched to using a central pipeline, what we call the factory in general, where we're all working more through filing tickets, the agents take care of it, so it's less running on our laptop. That created a different dynamic in the tech giant from the solo dev to actually product, engineering, sales, support, all working together. That's the transformation that we went through. According to recent reports, gunnar Grosch: I think we're seeing a similar thing that Patrick just described. There are different parts of the development lifecycle that are changing. I think part of it is about trusting it to be able to hand off things. I think we're seeing it in stages. One part that is easy to handle is the research part. Renato Losio: I don't know, really on a personal experience, I can say that if you talk to many practitioners it's, yes, we are experimenting with it. We are doing that. #23654. Removing binder.c

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1900 w)

Removing binder.c

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lwn

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that subscriptions are the lifeblood of LWN.net.
  • The final talk at Kangrejos 2026 was about the removal of the C implementation of Android's Binder driver, the primary interprocess communication mechanism used on Android devices.
  • Binder was added to the kernel in 2008, Llamas mentioned, as an interprocess communication mechanism for Android devices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that subscriptions are the lifeblood of LWN.net. If you appreciate this content and would like to see more of it, your subscription will help to ensure that LWN continues to thrive. Please visit this page to join up and keep LWN on the net.

The final talk at Kangrejos 2026 was about the removal of the C implementation of Android's Binder driver, the primary interprocess communication mechanism used on Android devices. Carlos Llamas announced that he had deleted the C code to general applause, and then shared some insights about what went into replacing the C implementation. Alice Ryhl, who has worked on the Rust implementation for some years, added her own thoughts about what the most difficult and interesting parts of the transition were.

Binder was added to the kernel in 2008, Llamas mentioned, as an interprocess communication mechanism for Android devices. Its design originated in BeOS, but it has grown significantly since then. It provides a rich set of operations for allowing processes to communicate with the minimum amount of overhead. It also, therefore, presents a large attack surface for Android. Many complicated chained attacks against Android have involved Binder at one step or another, Llamas explained. Google's internal "red team" (the team dedicated to proactive security research) deemed Binder to be the most vulnerability-dense component in the entire operating system, with more CVEs per line than anywhere else.

That made it an obvious candidate for porting to Rust, Llamas stated. Binder was the first user of Rust in the kernel, he added, although Ryhl did not publicly post the first version of what became the Rust implementation until 2023, well after the Rust experiment started in 2021. All told, the effort took more than five years. Binder is used for every single screen touch, permission check, and cross-application message on Android, which runs on more than three billion devices. In total, it works out to hundreds of billions of Binder transactions per second, globally, he added. That scale meant that even the smallest discrepancy between the interface provided by the C version and the one provided by the Rust version would cause problems and regressions for some use case.

One particularly tricky aspect has been performance, Ryhl stated. Throughput doesn't matter that much; what matters is the tail latencies. Most screen frames on Android have a Binder transaction in the critical path of the frame, she explained. So, a difference of two microseconds on average is not a real problem, but if Binder is ever twenty milliseconds slower, even once in a while, people will notice and care.

The actual algorithms that the C and Rust implementations use are identical, she continued, so there are no large differences in throughput. But, because Rust handles locking differently, there were problems with the tail latency from lock contention that she had to debug. For example, one user-reported traceback showed Binder attempting to take a mutex that was held by another process. That process was preempted, and did not resume executing for twenty milliseconds, well past the sixteen millisecond budget to render a single frame.

It was a classic case of priority inversion. To solve the problem in Binder, Ryhl moved as many operations out from under the lock as possible, and was able to replace it with a spinlock, which made the problem go away. The equivalent lock in the C implementation was already a spinlock: "I deviated from C Binder, and pow. It has eighteen years of accumulated quirks.".

Eventually, however, the Rust implementation was good enough for most use cases. And the C implementation was still producing new vulnerabilities every time someone tried to introduce a new feature. Eventually, Llamas and Ryhl decided to only add new features to the Rust implementation, in order to motivate people to switch and to avoid headaches from the C implementation. That policy has resulted in the Rust version becoming faster than the C version, because Ryhl was able to introduce an algorithmic improvement that reduced the number of needed system calls, a change that had been considered too complex for the C implementation. Now that the C implementation has been deleted, there are more of those coming, she promised.

In a recent development, another area that proved difficult was dealing with tracepoints. People aren't supposed to rely on the presence or behavior of most kernel-internal tracepoints, but they do. This meant that Ryhl had to copy the existing tracepoints in Binder as a de facto part of the driver's API. That even extended into some of the data structures involved in the driver. In one case, she said, there was a reference-counted structure that had a slightly different reference count in the Rust implementation, because the Rust code was holding an additional pointer to the structure. That turned out to be a problem for one particular piece of client code, since it relied on checking the reference count via a tracepoint in order to determine when the C implementation had reached a particular state.

In a recent development, there was also a lot of toolchain support needed, Ryhl continued. The Rust implementation had to work with kernel address-space layout randomization (KASLR), control-flow integrity (CFI), and profile-guided optimization. Production Android kernels are built with all of those enabled, and since they impact code generation, the Rust code needed to account for them.

Sources indicate that llamas then went into more detail about the deployment proposal that will be used to convert customers to the Rust implementation. A major problem with just rolling the Rust implementation out is the existence of vendor hooks: custom tracepoints used to inject vendor-specific behavior into the kernel. The Rust implementation of Binder was not able to reproduce those in every case, and therefore many vendors are stuck on the C implementation until they patch their code. That's going to be a slow process.

In a recent development, old stable versions of the kernel will continue to have the C Binder, and receive security fixes, which gives the various Android vendors a little bit of leeway until they're forced to update. After the conference, the patch removing the C implementation was merged as part of the 7.4 merge window, so that is the version past which the Rust implementation is required. 7.3 is the designated long-term-support release for 2026.

One person asked whether this would pose a problem for people compiling the kernel with GCC. Miguel Ojeda responded that many distributions are using a workaround for the current lack of Rust support in GCC: they are building the C side of the kernel with GCC, and the Rust side with LLVM. He stated that he had advised against compiling the kernel in that way, because it is "a complete hack", though people who use it are unlikely to complain about being forced onto Clang. Greg Kroah-Hartman added that it will take months or years to learn about anyone who has problems with the Rust version of the driver, given how slowly Android vendors upgrade their kernels. Furthermore, the removal is a single patch that can be cleanly reverted, if someone needs to continue using the C version.

Recent findings suggest that llamas thought that it was worth considering what the removal process should look like for other code that gets ported to Rust. He asked what people thought should happen to the C version of converted drivers on long-term-support branches. Ojeda said that the process would be exactly the same as the existing policy for replaced C code. The only difference between Rust and C in long-term-support releases is that the Rust maintainers backport fixes for soundness problems, he said. Kroah-Hartman told Llamas not to worry about code that has been replaced: "Just delete it. I take patches for subsystems that have been deleted. It's fine.".

Recent findings suggest that with that declaration, the session, the conference, and the presence of the C Binder driver in the kernel were all over. Binder is the first nontrivial component in the kernel to be ported to Rust, and its journey has revealed several pitfalls that don't apply to fresh drivers written in Rust from scratch. Still, the most difficult problems were not Rust-specific; they were the compatibility problems that any rewrite would face. Whether any other kernel components will find the hassle of a rewrite worth it, and how long they will take to accomplish it, remains to be seen.

[ Thanks to the Linux Foundation, LWN's travel sponsor, for supporting my travel to Kangrejos. ].

Sources indicate that this isn't a workaround, it's entirely normal. The C ABI is the same between GCC and LLVM. The only downside I'm aware of is that you can't do cross-language LTO this way.

According to recent reports, for the (large) subset of things that are standardized and ABI-defined, yes, but if there's e.g. an __attribute__((packed)) on a struct, using the same version of clang for your C compiler and for bindgen (in the form of libclang) can be expected to get it right, and there is no such expectation if it's two different compilers. And of course if you do something like enable a layout-changing plugin in GCC like randstruct, then this will definitely not work (though Kconfig prevents that particular mistake).

Sources indicate that it's equivalent to the reason that the standard advice is to use the exact same compiler for your kernel itself and for kernel modules. The ABI is supposed to be standard, but the kernel uses lots of language features and compiler-specific features.

(To be clear, I'm inclined to agree with you that it will generally work, and for over 20 years there has not actually been any enforcement that you did use the same compiler version.).

Aren't there codegen-affecting flags like CFI and such that are build options in the kernel? I imagine that needs compiler internal logic to match….

Industry observers note that aren't there codegen-affecting flags like CFI and such that are build options in the kernel? I imagine that needs compiler internal logic to match….

Codegen-affecting, yes, but are they ABI-affecting?

CFI is probably relaxed around anything that looks like an global-visibility symbol. What are other codegen-affecting options that involve nontrivial internal logic?

Sources indicate that other distributions like RHEL and SLES don't either. Is there a particular reason to single out Google here?

Industry observers note that I just bought a Samsung A27 (not a flagship), and Samsung promises 6 OS upgrades and 6 years of security updates. In this case (and probably others) the clock starts to run when a smartphone model appears globally, so it certainly is a good idea to look at the release year when comparing the update promises of different smart phones.

Sources indicate that if I search for 6 years of security updates, my favourite price comparison site lists smartphones from CMF, Honor, Motorola, Nothing, OnePlus, Oppo, Realme, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Xiaomi, so it's not just Samsung flagships. If you ask for 7 years instead, you get a different set of manufacturers (including Google); for 8 years, you get Fairphone. No one promises 9 or 10 years of security updates.

I previously had a Moto G100, gifted one year after it was released; it only had one more major Android release revision, and security fixes (which were already dripping at glacial pace) probably have finished too by now...

Tech Report: Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1387 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible.
  • Industry observers note that evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized.
  • Industry observers note that these arenas compare models by presenting users with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀.

Industry observers note that evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:.

Industry observers note that these arenas compare models by presenting users with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

It has been revealed that while human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously stated by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:.

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡.

Importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

Numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an important gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

Recent findings suggest that you can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

The “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is important for voice agents and other interactive apps.

For streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

Sources indicate that the default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

The goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

We will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Complications and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

Industry observers note that the check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS.".

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

According to recent reports, open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let users listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

According to recent reports, human feedback remains an crucial part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as upcoming TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and users better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

In a recent development, gitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard.

#23649. AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

📅 02 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2032 w)
