Latest Update: Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3317 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the upcoming US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Industry observers note that reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

Recent findings suggest that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

According to recent reports, beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

According to recent reports, beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

It has been revealed that hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

In a recent development, A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Blueprint for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

Industry observers note that the pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Recent findings suggest that beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Industry observers note that pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel strategy. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

It has been revealed that launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

According to recent reports, beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

Industry observers note that both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

It has been revealed that beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

It has been revealed that on Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

Recent findings suggest that * Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

Industry observers note that the setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

In a recent development, after one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

It has been revealed that reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can upgrade the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the latest weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

According to recent reports, the recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Industry observers note that enhancement: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Sources indicate that optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Recent findings suggest that evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

Industry observers note that the next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

Sources indicate that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

Industry observers note that at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

In a recent development, we used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

Industry observers note that you can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

According to recent reports, we wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

In a recent development, our score-versus-latency plot indicates the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

In a recent development, decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

Industry observers note that for a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Recent findings suggest that beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

Sources indicate that that’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Industry observers note that thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

Brad Wardell, Founder and CEO of Clairvoyance AI – Interview Series

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, brad Wardell is Founder and CEO of Clairvoyance AI and the founder and CEO of Stardock.
  • It has been revealed that clairvoyance AI develops a workspace for named AI staff with ongoing assignments and memory, connecting local files and development tools with cloud services and models running on a user’s own hardware.
  • You’ve spent more than three decades building desktop software and strategy games at Stardock, including products such as Fences and Galactic Civilizations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, brad Wardell is Founder and CEO of Clairvoyance AI and the founder and CEO of Stardock. He has spent more than three decades building desktop software and strategy games, including products such as Fences and Galactic Civilizations. His work on game development pipelines, creative assets, and everyday business reporting shaped his interest in persistent AI agents that can work directly with local files and applications.

It has been revealed that clairvoyance AI develops a workspace for named AI staff with ongoing assignments and memory, connecting local files and development tools with cloud services and models running on a user’s own hardware. Incubated at Stardock, it supports workflows that produce reusable notes, reports, and other artifacts. In this interview, Wardell discusses how game development informed the product, where local models fit into daily work, and the routing, memory, and permission controls needed to make agents useful.

You’ve spent more than three decades building desktop software and strategy games at Stardock, including products such as Fences and Galactic Civilizations. What problem inside your own business prompted you to build Clairvoyance AI, and when did you realize it could become a company of its own?

According to recent reports, the real pressure point was Ara: History Untold, which Stardock helped Microsoft and Oxide Games finish. A huge amount of time was going into just moving creative assets into the game. Writing came in as .DOCX files that had to be painstakingly hand-converted into XML or CSV. 3D assets had to be carefully brought into our engine. A single balance change meant touching a dozen different files. Localization meant matching translated strings back to the right keys in the right files by hand. Clairvoyance AI made all of that painless and let us ship on time.

Recent findings suggest that by late 2025, we had an internal debate about whether to make it public at all. It was a real competitive advantage, like having a superset of something like OpenClaw a year early. What pushed us toward going public was watching friends and colleagues lose jobs to AI automation that they could have kept if they’d had better tools. At that point, we knew we wanted to open Clairvoyance AI to the public.

You’ve argued that many AI agent tools reveal a lack of experience shipping consumer software. What mistakes do you see most often, and what lessons from your own career should AI developers be applying?

The biggest tell is terminology. If you don’t already know the words, like “glyph” for the little graphic on a button, you’re at a real disadvantage talking to an AI, because it’s trained on people who already know the lingo. Most of the teams building these tools are very smart but very young, and it shows in the usability choices. A good example is when Anthropic added the ability to drag text from one terminal session to another, that got millions of views. We’ve had agents that you can just @ by name to hand off work automatically, no dragging anything. Theirs requires the user to do the work the AI should be doing.

Industry observers note that the lesson from 30 years of shipping desktop software is that you have to actually use the thing you’re building, every day, with real deadlines, before anyone outside the company sees it. A lot of AI products feel like they were built by people who haven’t had to live inside their own software.

Recent findings suggest that you describe the next phase of AI as a routing problem: deciding what runs on a device, across a local network, or in the cloud. Could you walk us through a real workflow and explain how those decisions should be made?

Routing isn’t really an individual decision anymore, it’s becoming a manufacturer-level one. We’re about to release a feature called Hivemind that makes this concrete. Most enterprises already own plenty of capable machines that sit idle every night. Hivemind lets a company pool those idle GPUs across its own machines so anyone on the team can run AI work on them instead of sending it to the cloud. If you’re tracking tens of thousands of shipments across a supply chain, or auditing where a company’s money went, you don’t need a frontier cloud model for that. You need enough compute, and most companies already have it sitting unused after hours.

At the individual level, the same logic applies, just on a smaller scale. I run dashboards, crash reports, sentiment reports, and sales data every night on a local model instead of a cloud one. I used to run that same workload through Claude and it cost about $100 a month in tokens. Now it runs for free overnight on hardware I already own, and I read the results in the morning.

So the actual decision isn’t “local versus cloud,” it’s “does this need to happen while someone is staring at the screen, and does the organization already have the hardware to do it without paying per-token.”.

Industry observers note that you believe a substantial share of everyday agentic work can already run on local hardware. Which tasks have you demonstrated this with, on what hardware, and how do you measure success beyond whether a model produces a plausible answer?

We have had a lot of success with using local AI for adding metadata to our files. Like many companies, we have terabytes of data on our network. Stardock develops both software and games and on the game side, there’s decades of 3D and 2D art assets, videos, work products, etc.

Around the company we have a lot of pretty decent video cards from AMD and NVIDIA. We have found that 8B to 12B parameter models are more than enough to do everything we need and those will run on even relatively older hardware. Right now, we have a Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 laptop doing some of this work in the background during the evening.

It has been revealed that local AI is really good at just slowly chewing through and reviewing these files and adding metadata to it so that when we need to find something, you can search for it and find it promptly. Hence, we discovered that we have 16 different 3D models of wolves. Sigh.

According to recent reports, what should trigger escalation from a smaller local model to a more capable cloud model? How do you detect when the local model is struggling before it makes a consequential mistake?

In a recent development, right now, anything that requires open-ended judgement should probably go up to the cloud. The frontier models have largely solved hallucinations. When you go to smaller (local) models, hallucinations return. So on local models we tend to need to keep a lot of guardrails on them.

Recent findings suggest that clairvoyance organizes agents as AI staff with persistent memory and ongoing assignments. What have you learned about preserving useful context over time without allowing outdated instructions, incorrect assumptions, or conflicting memories to accumulate?

Industry observers note that under the covers, Clairvoyance stores its memories in a graph structure so when one thing updates, it tends to recursively trigger updates to other nodes. This helps ensure that the memories stay organized and up to date.

The challenge has been to prevent infinite recursion and that has required a lot of trial and error over the last couple of years.

Giving agents access to files, applications, and development tools makes them more useful, but also increases the consequences of errors. How do you structure permissions, human approvals, and recovery when an agent takes the wrong action?

The one concrete point we have is File Protection: Clairvoyance can block agents from wiping out directories, enforced at the app level rather than through hooks that an agent could work around.

When a workflow combines local execution with cloud inference, “local-first” can mean different things. What information leaves the user’s machine, and how can users understand and control that boundary?

Recent findings suggest that cloud security is about keeping other people out. It doesn’t answer whether the model provider should have your company’s secrets in the first place. Clairvoyance is local-first by design: your notes, projects, and staff memory live on your own machine. What goes to a cloud model is your call, made per staff member, not a blanket setting. Run a local model and nothing has to leave your hardware at all. We’re hearing this directly from enterprise customers who are frustrated about uploading entire confidential workflows to Anthropic or OpenAI just to get work done.

Recent findings suggest that clairvoyance has over 40,000 users. What have you learned from how people actually use Clairvoyance, and can you share a measurable example of a recurring workflow where it has delivered sustained value?

The retention rate is highly dependent on the amount of data the user is generating through their sessions.

Most customers of AI haven’t really crossed the threshold where they are taking the data the AI generates to build back onto it. Most users still think in terms of prompts. The users who stay with Clairvoyance are the ones generating a lot of Exhibits and Reports which in turn act as the foundation for further work.

It has been revealed that looking ahead a year, what developments would most expand the work agents can reliably handle locally? What would need to happen for you to reconsider your view that routing matters more than model size?

Sources indicate that I think within 18 months, 90 to 95% of AI work will be local, with maybe 5% needing the cloud for frontier work. That’s mostly because almost nothing is being delegated to AI yet, even trivial tasks like screening resumes for location or checking shipment timing are still done by hand, and a 4B model can already do that on a laptop. What expands this is Hivemind-style pooled compute (letting a company’s underused GPUs serve everyone on the domain) and routing getting good enough that nobody has to know what a 4B model or an Opus even is.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to try a desktop app for managing persistent AI agents across their computers should visit Clairvoyance AI.

Sources indicate that antoine is a visionary leader and founding partner of Unite.AI, driven by an unwavering passion for shaping and promoting the future of AI and robotics. A serial entrepreneur, he believes that AI will be as disruptive to society as electricity, and is often caught raving about the potential of disruptive technologies and AGI.

Industry observers note that as a futurist, he is dedicated to exploring how these innovations will shape our world. In addition, he is the founder of Securities.io, a platform focused on investing in cutting-edge technologies that are redefining the future and reshaping entire sectors.

TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (921 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that torchNeuron provides a upcoming native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
  • TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
  • 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that torchNeuron provides a upcoming native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

Industry observers note that to date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

It has been revealed that torchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

According to recent reports, for the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

Sources indicate that the following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Sources indicate that now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

According to recent reports, here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

The command below rolls out training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Sources indicate that many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

Sources indicate that more and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Sources indicate that make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, people can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

AI Can Scale Security. But Scale What?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprise security teams today face more activity, telemetry and alerts than they can realistically investigate manually.
  • In a recent development, for defenders, AI agents can change that equation by taking on investigations and other repetitive tasks across the environment.
  • An agent investigating millions of endpoints must understand what it is looking for, what constitutes unusual behavior in that particular environment and which findings warrant further investigation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Enterprise security teams today face more activity, telemetry and alerts than they can realistically investigate manually. Estimates vary, with some research suggesting the average security operations team receives more than 4,400 alerts a day. As organizations expand and add more tools, and AI enables more attacks, that number is bound to grow. We’re already seeing examples of enterprises that have two million endpoints in their environment, and security teams that are investigating these alerts manually are not fighting a fair fight against attackers that are increasingly agentic.

In a recent development, for defenders, AI agents can change that equation by taking on investigations and other repetitive tasks across the environment. However, the ability to process more data does not automatically translate into better threat detection or response. What’s needed is not just scale but context.

An agent investigating millions of endpoints must understand what it is looking for, what constitutes unusual behavior in that particular environment and which findings warrant further investigation. Without this context, automation risks scaling noise and generating irrelevant or misleading conclusions.

And it’s crucial to keep in mind that not every organization will be able to rely on frontier model investigations for each alert; that will get far too costly.

According to recent reports, security environments differ in their infrastructure, applications, operational requirements, regulatory obligations and risk tolerance. Defenders must keep applications running while managing compliance requirements and avoiding operational disruption.

To be effective, agents must incorporate organizational knowledge, including historical investigations, established procedures and the judgment of experienced analysts. Much of this knowledge isn’t something that can just be fed to an agent in a spreadsheet or other format; it’s something that needs to be observed in action, by learning from experienced defenders at work.

For enterprises, the significant question here is how to take that institutional knowledge and translate it into systems capable of making consistent, contextually appropriate decisions at machine speed.

Organizations need mechanisms to capture and apply the knowledge that informs investigations, including previous case decisions, established procedures and how analysts interpret evidence. Enterprises may have “custom” types of processes, tools and tribal knowledge that need to be captured, as well.

Sources indicate that model specialization is one potential approach. Fine-tuning models for individual enterprise customers can support large-scale investigations at a more predictable cost while maintaining strong performance. Fine-tuned open-source models may be particularly useful for tasks involving very large endpoint populations.

Organizations must also evaluate agent performance as models, workflows and enterprise environments change. Synthetic environments, or digital twins, can provide representative settings for testing different agent versions when production data is no longer available or has become outdated.

Fine-tuning is not the only way to provide context. Retrieval, memory, workflow orchestration and explicit policy controls are alternative approaches. The central requirement is that the chosen method improves an agent’s performance in the environment where it will operate.

Correctly identifying a threat is only part of the challenge. Agents must understand which actions they are authorized to take, when human approval is necessary and how to avoid disrupting legitimate business operations. Determining where agents can act autonomously and where human decision-making is required is essential to trusted deployment.

Industry observers note that autonomy at scale also requires economy of scale. Companies that use frontier models for millions of investigations are going to bankrupt themselves. That makes finding the most efficient method of investigating with an AI model, whether a Small Language Model (SLM) or a proprietary one, paramount.

Sources indicate that autonomy should be proportionate to risk. Routine, well-understood tasks may be suitable for autonomous execution, while consequential or disruptive actions may require human approval or additional authorization. Enterprise security also depends on coordination across teams. An investigation that identifies a threat requiring a firewall configuration change must transition seamlessly to the team responsible for that system, with appropriate authorization and accountability for remediation.

Governance and workflow design are therefore essential components of agent deployment, not controls that can be added after the technology has been scaled.

Organizations should assess agents using outcome-based measures, including investigation accuracy, false-positive and false-negative rates, time to investigate and remediate, cost per investigation, escalation quality and adherence to authorization policies.

Continuous evaluation is essential as models and workflows change. Testing different agent versions against representative cases and using synthetic environments can help organizations identify regressions before deploying updates into production.

Recent findings suggest that security leaders must balance the benefits of automation against the operational risks of deployment. Application availability, compliance obligations, organizational risk tolerance and implementation timelines all influence how promptly latest capabilities can be adopted.

AI offers security teams an opportunity to address a longstanding capacity problem, but raw scale is not the end goal. The real opportunity lies in combining machine speed with organizational context, appropriate authority and human judgment so agents can distinguish what matters, take the right actions and involve the right people when necessary.

Tech Report: MPS in PyTorch 2.15

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • Industry observers note that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and upcoming Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

Industry observers note that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Recent findings suggest that every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the major matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

In a recent development, MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

It has been revealed that in 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

It has been revealed that the decoding kernel demonstrates up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Industry observers note that small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

Recent findings suggest that SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them latest paths through Metal:.

Sources indicate that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

In a recent development, you can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Sources indicate that work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Industry observers note that scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

Industry observers note that I was in California, in Silicon Valley, for about 25 years, when Tesco reached out to me, saying, would you like to work at Tesco? I had got no concept of Tesco, because I had never come to London before that. When I looked at the website, it was a pretty basic website. The outside-in perspective, when you look at the website of a large grocery chain, feels like there is no technology. This went on for a few months. After that, they convinced me to talk to a few people in the technology department. The state that this technology was, and what was needed for growth and the transformation that was needed at scale, was what motivated me and my wife. We were empty nesters already by that time. We decided, why not? Came here. Just around that time, Trump got elected. We felt even better.

Recent findings suggest that first of all, some context into how large Tesco is. There are about 5,000 stores. Some of them are super. Some of them are medium. Some of them are small. They are across five different countries. We used to be in Asia as well, when I started 10 years back, in Thailand, Malaysia. We divested those businesses. We are still in five countries. We have 20 distribution centers. We have 25 million customers. That's almost one-third of the UK population. That's not small. We have 350,000 colleagues across our stores. Out of that, maybe around 15,000 in head office. Out of that, around 6,000 in technology. Again, it's significant. It's big operations, large number of colleagues. We do around 50 million baskets. Not number of transactions, the baskets, which means the orders across our estate in our stores. We do 1.3 million online orders in a week. When COVID came, many companies talk about scale.

When COVID happened, when entire business shifted towards online, our challenge was to double the number of online slots that we can make available for our customers. By that time, for the e-commerce part, our platform was already live. When we doubled it, that's equivalent of putting almost three other competitor companies online in one month. Many companies stopped taking orders. Many companies stopped signing customers. We doubled it in a month. That again shows the scale. Fifty million cases through supply chain, huge. We are not even talking about number of miles the trucks travel and the logistics within the distribution center. We do 4.5 billion calls a day. We have 98% UK coverage when I talk about 25 million customers, but coverage-wise in terms of online business, that can cover the entire geography of UK. We cover almost 98%, which means you can have your home delivery of grocery done in 98% of the UK.

Tills, as we call it here in the UK, POS systems, as called in many other countries, almost 50,000. That's just POS devices. We are not talking about all other thousands and tens of thousands of handheld devices that run on the same platform. That's just the context, because that sets a very different tone for the kind of technology, how mission-critical technology becomes. Then driving transformation through that is quite challenging, because I worked at startups. I've worked at mid-size companies. I had my own startup. Being in California and not having a startup is a crime. I tried that, too. I worked at Yahoo for 10 years. I worked at large companies, worked at startups. Tesco is yet another scale. I wanted to reflect here, because it drives quite a lot of complexities in decision-making of what would you do with your transformation and technology choices.

Sources indicate that this goes beyond retail. Any industry that has got physical estate, digital, and real-time operations will face these complexities. That's where we learned about being both efficient and effective. Efficient is do things well, fast. Effective, do good things, which are more effective. A slight difference in nuances. You can be doing fast all the things, but if those are not the right things, you are chasing wrong goals. Do the right things and do things the right way, efficiency and effectiveness. I wanted to share here, this is not just about retail. This will apply to many of the industries who operate at that kind of scale and complexity.

Let's start as to why. Ten years back, why did we need transformation? It was quite a poor state within technology I'm talking. When they talked about a large grocery company and I was thinking there is no technology inside, there was a lot of technology, but it was very siloed. Multiple technology stacks tied to historical business structures. When I'm talking siloed, this is not just, store had a POS system and e-commerce had something else. I'm talking multiple stacks within online or e-commerce business itself. Grocery, its entire stack. We had marketplace back then, completely different stack. One Microsoft, .NET, one Oracle. F&F, our clothing, Tesco wine. Customers across these, forget having single account, did not even have single login. Jayesh@groceryhomeshopping is different than Jayesh@marketplace, is different than Jayesh@f&f. We had no single customer view, no data platforms, no product management, nothing. It was that fragmented. There was no single identity, as I just explained.

In a recent development, no single source of truth for stock or pricing. From that perspective, when you have multiple monolithic systems running in private data centers, we were not in public cloud back then. It was not even private data cloud. It was just a bunch of machines. You would be lucky if you asked for a server and you get a server in two months. That was the state. Decades old POS system, 20 years old software running on our POS systems in the stores, completely batch oriented. You couldn't connect to them. The deployments were the engineers would go with the floppy disk and then will deploy the software in the stores. Third-party solutions, not just third-party solutions, they were heavily customized, because when you are at the scale of Tesco, you can demand saying, I need a slightly different thing in your software. Sounds good initially. Then you're locked in with a very customized version of vendor solution for multiple years.

We had software running from vendor solutions that were at least a decade old. You can't even upgrade them. Then heavily outsourced resources as well. These were where we had lots of consulting firms providing resources for us. Not a good culture, not good quality. You can imagine what the landscape was when we started 10 years back. At the scale of Tesco, that becomes quite complex to say, how do you find your journey through that?

That got us the imperative for change, saying we definitely need omnichannel experience, because customer expectations were moving very fast. The old style of doing business was not working. Technology was not helping business. Business had all the motivation to change. Technology was stuck. We had hit the wall, literally. Global coherence across physical and digital estate, both. Rapid change cycles. Back then, as I said, if you talked to a vendor and asked for a solution in our POS systems, it would be six months for minor changes. Regression on top of that, so three things would be broken. You do the testing, and they charge you for fixing the bugs again. It would be six to nine months before you could get anything out on our Tills or POS systems in stores. Forget e-commerce. Then along with that, of course, we needed higher reliability, higher capability. We needed omnichannel experience, higher security, everything.

It needed more capability and capacity, both. That led to us chasing from fragmented stacks to unified platforms that could serve all our channels across all our markets and develop a multi-tenant platform. That's what we developed. It was called only platform. Sometimes platform terms are confusing. I'm not talking just the tech platform. I'm talking about the retail platform that runs our business. We'll talk about tech platform as well. That's part of our learning as to how tech platforms are super key if you don't start early. When we started, it was a retail platform to say, how do we now enable all these businesses and develop the retail platform?

In a recent development, where are we now? All of our entire UK business and Republic of Ireland business runs on this platform, 100%. We are making inroads in our Central European businesses. There are multiple countries there. They all have their nuances. The trust in technology is much higher. Technology strategy is very well integrated with the business strategy. It's not like service-oriented mindset of say, we just need three things. Go ahead and can you build it? That's how the siloed happened long time back. We'll talk about that in our transformation journey. As I said, the platform is much more scalable but also capable. That's where we are now. We'll talk about how we are looking into the future of agentic commerce from that perspective. Technology has become an integral part of the entire business ecosystem. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Companies are giving AI a bigger role in decisions, but that does not mean their leaders find decisions easier. In a survey published by Körber, 76% of senior decision-makers noted decision-making had become more complex. The same share reported allowing AI to play a greater role. The answers describe two trends happening at the same time; they do not establish that one caused the other.

In a recent development, the survey included 2,000 senior executives, split evenly between the United States and Germany. Körber claims respondents worked for organizations with annual revenue above $250 million and at least 250 employees, and fieldwork ran from August 27 to September 8, 2026. That makes the findings a look at decision-making inside larger organizations in two markets, not a representative measure of every employer or of small businesses.

Industry observers note that the accompanying release claims 74% of respondents reported that information volume can get in the way of decisions, while 75% remarked decisions stall when critical information is not available at the right time. Having more data and having the right data when a decision is due are different problems.

Consider a manager who needs to decide whether to delay a shipment. Sales, warehouse operations and finance may have different records for the same order, all updated at different times. An AI assistant can summarize those records promptly, but a faster summary does not establish which number is current or who can approve an exception. Unless the team can check the sources and resolve conflicting records, the tool can move the work of reconciliation from one person to another rather than eliminate it.

Recent findings suggest that the survey also found that 73% of respondents were uncomfortable letting technology make the final decision. That helps explain why businesses may want AI in the workflow without giving it control of the outcome. Drafting an explanation, gathering supporting documents and making a decision that commits the organization are separate jobs. The cost of an error differs for each.

Industry observers note that among respondents whose organizations described their transformation as enterprise-wide, 63.8% reported strong organizational performance, compared with 41.6% of those at the pilot stage. Future-readiness confidence was 66.4% and 46.5%, respectively. Aims to invest significantly in AI decision support were almost identical: 59% for the enterprise-wide group, versus 59.4% for the pilot group.

Those are self-reported group differences, not measured returns from a controlled rollout. Organizations that can implement technology across departments may already have stronger data, more resources or better operating processes. The publication does not establish that expanding a pilot causes performance to improve. It is better read as a prompt to ask what mature implementations do differently and which of those practices a particular team can test.

According to recent reports, the practical question for an operator is where a tool improves the work between a question and a decision. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework offers a way to formalize responsibilities and decide what to measure in context. Teams can pick a recurring decision and compare how long it takes to obtain the necessary evidence, how often a recommendation must be corrected and whether an approver can explain what they relied on.

Recent findings suggest that tracking these measures separately can reveal a trade-off that a single adoption number misses. A tool may produce reports faster while increasing the time spent checking them, or it may let people spend less time gathering facts and more time evaluating options. For the executives surveyed, the challenge is not simply making AI more available. It is defining the role it plays when information is incomplete and someone still has to own the decision.

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this newly introduced generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too major to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the upcoming provider can't replay them.

Recent findings suggest that API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

Recent findings suggest that while we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

Recent findings suggest that the first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

According to recent reports, and if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Sources indicate that community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Databricks has added PostgreSQL 19 to Lakebase and Neon, giving teams a way to try the open-source database’s upcoming maintenance, query planning and replication tools on managed infrastructure.
  • Industry observers note that the update is relevant to teams building AI applications, even though it does not introduce a new AI model or vector index.
  • One of the main additions in the PostgreSQL 19 release is REPACK, a command that rebuilds a table to reclaim unused space and can optionally reorder the data to match an index.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Databricks has added PostgreSQL 19 to Lakebase and Neon, giving teams a way to try the open-source database’s upcoming maintenance, query planning and replication tools on managed infrastructure. Databricks states both services had support on the day the PostgreSQL project released the new version. PostgreSQL’s own announcement dates the community release to November 19, 2026.

Industry observers note that the update is relevant to teams building AI applications, even though it does not introduce a new AI model or vector index. Operational databases often sit behind the user-facing parts of these systems. They store conversation history, track jobs and permissions, record application events and serve calls that need predictable response times. A database upgrade that makes this infrastructure easier to maintain can matter more to those teams than a new feature in the application layer.

One of the main additions in the PostgreSQL 19 release is REPACK, a command that rebuilds a table to reclaim unused space and can optionally reorder the data to match an index. PostgreSQL creates a fresh row version when data changes. Routine vacuuming makes old space available for reuse, but that does not always shrink the underlying table on disk. A table that stores frequently updated jobs or messages can keep occupying more space than its remaining live rows need.

According to recent reports, an option lets ordinary reads and writes continue through most of the rebuild. That does not make the operation free of disruption. As Neon’s release notes explain, PostgreSQL still needs an exclusive lock to finish swapping the rebuilt files into place. Teams should test the operation under a representative write load rather than assume the final lock is negligible on a busy table.

The release also adds pg_plan_advice, an extension for testing and stabilizing execution intends, and a companion pg_stash_advice extension that can apply stored advice to a matching query. The planner ordinarily chooses how to execute a query based on the data and statistics available. When that choice changes, an operation that used to be fast can suddenly become slow. The new tools give operators a way to investigate or mitigate that regression without immediately rewriting application code. Any saved advice should be revisited as the data and workload evolve.

Industry observers note that postgreSQL 19 also adds WAIT FOR LSN, which lets an application wait for a database replica to reach a specified position in the write-ahead log. With asynchronous replication, a write can succeed on the primary database before a replica has applied it. A user or agent that immediately reads from that replica may otherwise see an earlier state.

That lag matters if, for example, an application records approval for a task and immediately asks another service to read it from a replica. Waiting for the relevant log position can let that read see the approval. It trades some waiting time for freshness when the workflow needs it, rather than assuming all replica reads are current.

Databricks’ supported-versions documentation lists PostgreSQL 19 for Lakebase, and Neon’s announcement explains how to choose it for a latest project. Neither announcement says that all existing databases were automatically upgraded. Databricks also says Lakebase engineers contributed to the upstream release, including work on query-plan advice, shared memory and release management.

According to recent reports, for teams considering a migration, version availability is a starting point. A useful test is to run representative queries, confirm extension compatibility, measure replica lag and rehearse the maintenance operations that prompted the upgrade. Teams can then compare those results with the behavior of their current database before switching production traffic.
