💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • It has been revealed that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

It has been revealed that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch customers had to work harder to get in.

Industry observers note that until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

According to recent reports, to make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

It has been revealed that torchTPU adds TPU as a newly introduced backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Sources indicate that models too major for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

Industry observers note that the Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

According to recent reports, TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

Sources indicate that the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

In a recent development, decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

Sources indicate that we're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

Industry observers note that it's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

Recent findings suggest that TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch customers. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

Sources indicate that we can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

Default settings and sharing permissions determine whether those distinctions are easy for staff to maintain.

An institution still needs to assess what can be submitted to each model, how records are retained and whether its agreements address the kinds of information staff handle.

A university might track how much time staff save drafting course materials, while an agency might count how often a model summary needs substantive correction. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • It has been revealed that this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

It has been revealed that this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

According to recent reports, the modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

It has been revealed that start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table demonstrates that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

In a recent development, the table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

Sources indicate that in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

In a recent development, in eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In a recent development, in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

In a recent development, with @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

Recent findings suggest that the table reveals one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

Tech Report: Andrew Nassar, CTO of IC Realtime – Interview Series

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2206 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andrew Nassar is CTO of IC Realtime, where he has helped guide the organization through shifts from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and AI-assisted video analysis.
  • It has been revealed that IC Realtime designs video surveillance systems and software for residential and commercial environments.
  • Recent findings suggest that you’ve helped lead IC Realtime through the transitions from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and now AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andrew Nassar is CTO of IC Realtime, where he has helped guide the organization through shifts from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and AI-assisted video analysis. With more than 20 years in the surveillance industry, he focuses on turning advances in computer vision and edge computing into practical tools for understanding events, finding footage, and improving security operations.

It has been revealed that IC Realtime designs video surveillance systems and software for residential and commercial environments. Its Bunker platform adds AI analysis to compatible camera systems through a dedicated NVIDIA Jetson-powered gateway, supporting contextual alerts and natural-language video search. The platform combines local analysis with cloud-connected services for remote access and video history.

Recent findings suggest that you’ve helped lead IC Realtime through the transitions from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and now AI. What convinced you that AI could fundamentally change surveillance, and what advances have made sophisticated video analysis practical at the edge?

It has been revealed that we have worked with machine learning and computer vision on our cameras for years. The opportunity became much more useful when the system could help someone understand an event and find the relevant footage, rather than simply produce more video to review. A homeowner wants to know what deserves attention. A business wants to find an incident without spending hours searching.

Bunker brings that approach to a dedicated NVIDIA Jetson gateway at the property. Moving core analysis closer to the cameras can reduce the dependence on sending every analytical task to the cloud and improve responsiveness. The practical advance is the combination of local computing and software that turns video into contextual alerts and searchable events.

My standard is still proven value. The technology has to solve a real problem in the environment where the customer will use it. A good demonstration is the beginning of that process.

It has been revealed that using Bunker as an example, could you walk us through what happens between a camera capturing an event and a user receiving an alert? Which AI functions run locally, what still requires the cloud, and what data leaves the property?

At a high level, a compatible camera sends video to the Bunker Gateway, and core AI analysis happens on that gateway at the property. The platform links detected activity to video events and can send a contextual alert with a snapshot and a plain-language description. The user can then review the video in the app.

Bunker uses a hybrid architecture. Cloud connectivity supports remote access, subscription services and video history, so it would be misleading to call the platform cloud-free or to say no video leaves the property. What matters is how that data is protected when it does leave. Everything is encrypted in transit, including live video, which stays encrypted from the gateway all the way to the viewer’s screen. The infrastructure in between relays it but can’t watch it. Each gateway authenticates with its own certificate, never shared credentials, and footage stored in the cloud is encrypted.

Customers should get a clear explanation of that flow, including which features depend on the internet and what happens when the connection is down.

Security cameras operate in rain, darkness, glare, and constantly changing environments. What is the hardest real-world failure you’ve encountered, and how do you measure whether improvements reduce false alarms without increasing missed incidents?

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been in this industry for more than 20 years, and camera technology has improved dramatically, especially in low light and difficult conditions. Nighttime and noisy images are now nearly as clear as daytime. Even so, rain, glare, fog and snow can still reduce an AI model’s accuracy. Better sensors don’t remove those variables.

So we chose a dynamic approach that adjusts to changing environments and times of day, rather than relying on one fixed configuration. Over the past two years of development, we’ve put thousands of hours into testing in real-world installations, not just cameras on a bench, and we’ve built the system around what those deployments taught us.

It has been revealed that I wouldn’t judge an improvement by a lower notification count alone. The question is whether it removes irrelevant alerts while still catching the incidents that matter. Reducing noise is only valuable if the system stays useful when something important happens.

Detecting a person or vehicle is different from deciding that behavior is concerning. How do you define an anomaly, adapt that definition to each location, and prevent the system from treating harmless activity as a threat?

Industry observers note that A detected object does not, by itself, tell you whether there is a problem. A delivery at the front entrance and activity in a restricted area can involve the same type of object but require very different responses. The starting point should be the customer’s use case and the context of that particular property.

Sources indicate that I would distinguish an event worth reviewing from a conclusion that someone is a threat. The system should help a person understand what was observed and why it was surfaced, with access to the underlying footage. It should not encourage the user to treat every unfamiliar activity as evidence of wrongdoing.

As these systems become more capable, the challenge is to make that context useful without overstating what the AI knows. Human judgment remains crucial, particularly when an alert could lead to a consequential action.

It has been revealed that natural-language search promises to replace hours of manually reviewing footage. How does your system connect a user’s description to the right video, and how do you test for missed events, incorrect matches, or AI-generated descriptions that the footage doesn’t support?

The concept is to make video searchable in the language a person would naturally use. As activity is detected, Bunker creates time-stamped descriptions associated with video events. A user’s question is used to search that indexed record and surface relevant footage. That gives the user a starting point without manually scrubbing through the entire recording.

The footage should remain the basis for checking the result. A generated description is useful for navigation, but it should not be treated as more authoritative than what the camera actually captured.

For testing, I would separate three questions: Did the system miss a relevant event? Did it retrieve something that does not match the request? Did the description include something the footage does not support? Those are different failure modes. Evaluating only whether the search returns a plausible-looking answer would not be enough.

What trade-offs does NVIDIA Jetson hardware impose on model size, accuracy, power consumption, and the number of camera feeds you can analyze? How do you maintain reliable performance when using older third-party cameras, reaching processing capacity, or losing internet connectivity?

The design question is how to deliver useful analysis within the resources available at the property. Model complexity, the amount of video being processed and the required response time all have to fit the gateway’s operating limits. That is why the number of supported streams alone does not tell the whole performance story.

Bunker’s launch aims support up to 10 camera streams. Compatible ONVIF cameras let customers keep their existing hardware, but compatibility still needs to be verified for each installation. Profiles, firmware, image quality and the features being used all matter.

According to recent reports, we also need to be precise about resilience. Local processing and cloud-connected services are different parts of the system, and having an edge gateway doesn’t mean every feature works normally during an internet outage. Updates are part of reliability too. Every enhancement is signed and verified on the gateway before it installs, older vulnerable versions are rejected, and a failed update rolls back automatically. A bad update shouldn’t be what takes a property’s security system offline.

Local inference alone doesn’t answer every privacy question. Where does Bunker store footage, search queries, and AI-generated metadata, how long are they retained, and who can access them? How do you improve your models without assuming access to customers’ private footage?

It has been revealed that footage and the databases behind the service are encrypted at rest. Passwords are hashed and sessions expire, so even a database breach wouldn’t give anyone working logins. The gateway itself is encrypted too, so a stolen device yields no footage and no credentials. Bunker’s launch offering included 60 days of cloud video history on Standard and 365 days on Premium, plus Video Vault for clips a customer chooses to save.

It has been revealed that we don’t use customer footage to train our models, and we don’t create biometric templates of anyone the cameras capture. A customer using the product is not permission for us to reuse their private video.

The controversy surrounding Flock Safety has highlighted questions about who can search surveillance data and whether access is properly revoked. Although your deployment model differs, what lessons apply to your systems, and which safeguards should be mandatory rather than optional?

The backlash against Flock isn’t really about the AI. It’s about who can get in and search the data. Much of the scrutiny came down to account security, including lawmakers asking why multi-factor authentication wasn’t mandatory. When a stolen password is enough to search a surveillance system, it doesn’t matter where the model runs.

It has been revealed that with Bunker, the only people with access to a system’s data are the people that system’s owner has granted access. We don’t share it with third parties, we don’t use customer data to train our models, and we don’t create biometric templates.

Industry observers note that security has to start at the device and carry through to the account. Every Bunker gateway ships with its own cryptographic identity, so there are no default passwords to change or for an attacker to look up. Firmware is verified at every boot, updates are signed and checked before they install, and logins are protected with multi-factor authentication. Beyond that, access should be removed promptly when it’s no longer needed, and sensitive activity should leave an auditable record. Trust depends on being able to explain who did what.

According to recent reports, people captured by a camera often aren’t the people who bought it. How should AI surveillance account for the privacy of neighbors, employees, visitors, and passersby, and are there capabilities you would deliberately refuse to build?

In a recent development, the installation needs a defined purpose, and that purpose should guide what is captured, what is analyzed and who can see the results. Wanting to secure an entrance doesn’t mean every activity on a neighboring property should become part of a searchable record.

In a recent development, one line we’ve drawn is identity. Bunker doesn’t create biometric templates, and it doesn’t attach an identity to anyone it detects. It describes what happened, not who someone is. That keeps the system focused on events rather than on tracking or profiling people.

More capability doesn’t automatically mean more value. If a feature creates a serious trust problem without solving a clear customer problem, that’s a reason not to build it.

Looking ahead three to five years, what meaningful capability do you expect edge AI to unlock beyond today’s detection and search—and what technical or trust problem must be solved before it deserves widespread adoption?

Honestly, the future of AI is uncharted right now, and it’s moving faster than anything I’ve seen in my career. We’re following those changes almost daily and looking at where they can genuinely benefit the people using our platform.

The areas that matter most to us are context, understanding, and systems that keep learning and improving. The value is in helping someone understand a developing situation and decide what needs attention, instead of piecing together a string of separate notifications.

The technical challenge is to do that reliably in changing environments and within the limits of the local hardware. The trust challenge is to make the system’s limits and data practices easy to understand. People need to know what it observed, what it inferred and when a human needs to make the call.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore professional security cameras, recorders, and AI-powered video surveillance systems should visit IC Realtime.

Antoine is a visionary leader and founding partner of Unite.AI, driven by an unwavering passion for shaping and promoting the future of AI and robotics. A serial entrepreneur, he believes that AI will be as disruptive to society as electricity, and is often caught raving about the potential of disruptive technologies and AGI.

It has been revealed that as a futurist, he is dedicated to exploring how these innovations will shape our world. In addition, he is the founder of Securities.io, a platform focused on investing in cutting-edge technologies that are redefining the future and reshaping entire sectors.

#23601. Industry News: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2212 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2212 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

In a recent development, one of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

Industry observers note that we rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

According to recent reports, the leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

It has been revealed that the first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

According to recent reports, the second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

Industry observers note that to see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

Sources indicate that the third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a newly introduced idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

According to recent reports, first, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Industry observers note that second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping tech giant: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

In a recent development, to find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Industry observers note that third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

Sources indicate that an expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents demonstrates up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

Industry observers note that to measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

Recent findings suggest that the model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

According to recent reports, the lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

According to recent reports, vocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

Industry observers note that vocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Huawei used its November 20, 2026 brand event to introduce OSTA (星芒), a new smartphone sub-brand, and launch the O1 Pro as a HarmonyOS AI phone with a starting list price of CNY 5,699.
  • In a recent development, the new brand’s first handset makes Huawei’s own software and assistant its defining features.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.
  • According to recent reports, google has announced it is donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), placing two important components of its AI agent infrastructure under vendor-neutral open-source governance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Google Donates Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF to Secure AI Agents at Scale.

Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.

According to recent reports, google has announced it is donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), placing two important components of its AI agent infrastructure under vendor-neutral open-source governance. The move is intended to address two emerging challenges in running autonomous agents at scale: securely executing untrusted, AI-generated code and managing the substantial compute overhead created by agents that frequently pause and resume.

In a recent development, the announcement also includes OpenRL, Google's open-source reinforcement learning orchestration project. Together, the projects target different layers of agent infrastructure, from isolated code execution to managing agent lifecycles and coordinating large-scale training workloads. The goal is to establish an open foundation for agentic applications, much as Kubernetes helped standardise container orchestration.

Google argues that conventional Kubernetes workloads and AI agents have fundamentally different execution patterns.

A traditional application typically starts, serves requests, and continues running. An AI agent, however, may execute a tool or code for a few seconds before waiting for model inference, an external API, or human approval. Google estimates that agents can spend 90-95% of their time idle while still holding notable state, including memory, files, repositories, and active sessions.

Keeping every agent in a dedicated Pod wastes resources, while scaling to zero introduces delays when environments must be reconstructed. At the other extreme, large-scale agent evaluations can overwhelm Kubernetes control planes when thousands of short-lived execution environments are repeatedly created and destroyed.

Google developed Agent Substrate to address these limitations by separating agent state (actors) from the compute resources (workers) used to execute it.

Recent findings suggest that actors represent individual agent sessions and retain their state, including filesystem contents, memory, and execution context. Workers provide reusable, pre-warmed execution environments drawn from shared Kubernetes pools.

Industry observers note that when an agent needs to resume, Substrate assigns it to an available Worker and restores its previous state. When the agent becomes idle, its state can be saved and the underlying compute resource released.

According to Google, this approach lets agents resume in under 500 milliseconds without creating a newly introduced Kubernetes Pod for every execution. It also reduces pressure on the Kubernetes control plane by managing agent lifecycles independently of individual Pod objects.

It has been revealed that the second major challenge is security. AI agents routinely execute generated shell commands, install packages, and interact with external tools. Treating this code as trusted creates significant risks, particularly when multiple agents share infrastructure.

Industry observers note that google's gVisor provides an additional isolation boundary through a user-space application kernel. Instead of letting containerised applications interact directly with the host Linux kernel, gVisor intercepts system calls and handles them within its own isolated environment.

This reduces the exposure of the underlying host while retaining much of the efficiency associated with container-based execution.

Agent Substrate also supports Cloud Hypervisor microVMs for workloads requiring hardware-level virtualisation. This gives platform teams flexibility to select an appropriate isolation boundary without changing the overall agent lifecycle model.

In a recent development, the announcement reflects a broader shift in cloud-native infrastructure. Kubernetes was designed around long-running applications and relatively stable workloads. Agentic systems introduce more dynamic execution patterns, where environments must be created, suspended, restored, and isolated at much greater frequency.

Other providers are addressing similar challenges through technologies such as Kata Containers, Firecracker, and dedicated sandboxing platforms. Google's contribution is to combine secure execution with an agent-aware orchestration model and place the resulting technologies within an open ecosystem.

According to recent reports, the wider implication is that AI agents need more than an orchestration framework and access to tools; they need their own secure, stateful, and efficiently managed execution infrastructure. By donating these projects to the CNCF, Google is helping establish the foundations for that next layer of cloud-native computing.

Tech Report: Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done.
  • Sources indicate that we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
  • ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

Sources indicate that we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

In a recent development, figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

In a recent development, then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

Recent findings suggest that we call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

Industry observers note that we used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

According to recent reports, table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

Industry observers note that in our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

According to recent reports, and bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

Industry observers note that if you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 highlights which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

In a recent development, after training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

According to recent reports, the headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

According to recent reports, average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

In a recent development, figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

According to recent reports, pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

Recent findings suggest that table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

It has been revealed that figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

It has been revealed that the dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Industry observers note that figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

In a recent development, every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Industry observers note that training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each enhancement generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

According to recent reports, zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

It has been revealed that that explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

In a recent development, no ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

It has been revealed that why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

Sources indicate that A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Sources indicate that each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

It has been revealed that we partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

It has been revealed that figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

Sources indicate that figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

Sources indicate that when an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.
